📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Federal Aviation Administration said Tuesday it would pause the installation of latest routers after problems with the technology led the agency to issue a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday.
  • Tens of thousands of flights were affected by the ground stop, which halted departing flights for more than four hours.
  • Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Sunday that an overloaded router installed in southern Arkansas as part of an upgrade to a system overseen by L3Harris Technologies appeared to overwhelm systems that feed radar and other data for air traffic control.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Federal Aviation Administration said Tuesday it would pause the installation of latest routers after problems with the technology led the agency to issue a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday.

Tens of thousands of flights were affected by the ground stop, which halted departing flights for more than four hours. It was the longest halt to U.S. flight departures since 9/11.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Sunday that an overloaded router installed in southern Arkansas as part of an upgrade to a system overseen by L3Harris Technologies appeared to overwhelm systems that feed radar and other data for air traffic control.

The Wall Street Journal first reported the news about the pause.

The FAA and Department of Transportation have stated L3Harris was working to convert the communications network from copper wires to fiber optic.

Democratic members of the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science and Transportation this week asked the FAA and the Department of Transportation for clarity on what went wrong.

Recent findings suggest that "Identifying the device that failed does not establish why it failed," the senators wrote in a statement. "Modernization cannot come at the expense of operational safety.".

The agencies have said they are working to figure out the root cause of the concern and have reiterated that there is no indication of a cyberattack or outside threat.

The senators also asked for a briefing with the FAA, L3Harris and Juniper Networks, which is making the new devices, by Monday. They asked the companies to lay out why the operational systems lacked sufficient redundancy and answer other questions about what led to the outage.

CNBC has reached out to L3Harris and Juniper Networks for comment.

Duffy on Friday called for Congress to approve $50 billion in funding for upgrades to the aging U.S. air traffic control system, more than he has previously asked for. Democratic lawmakers pushed back on the request, citing unspent money from existing funding, which includes Congress' approval last year of $12.5 billion for airport and air traffic control improvements over five years.

Senate Commerce Chair Ted Cruz, R-Texas, said Tuesday that he thinks there will be support for air traffic control modernization, but that the allocation should be specifically for safety upgrades.

Sources indicate that "I don't think the full $50 billion will be funded," he said. "Some of that is not safety related, but we just discussed there, and what I expressed is that the request needs to be focused on safety modernization.".

According to recent reports, duffy dismissed the idea that the router glitch had to do with the introduction of artificial intelligence tools and mentioned it was "completely unfounded" because the AI system is not in communication with the defective router. He added that the FBI is helping to investigate the root cause of the issue.

Aging equipment and a shortage of air traffic controllers have for years angered airline executives, who have complained about the cost of resulting disruptions.

— CNBC's Phil LeBeau, Leslie Josephs and Justin Papp contributed to this report.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hearts' hopes of a memorable draw with Monaco were dashed in the 94th minute.

There was a bittersweet feeling at Tynecastle after Folarin Balogun's 94th-minute winner preserved Monaco's perfect Conference League record and condemned Hearts to a third defeat from four.

Wouter Vrancken's side had gone toe-to-toe with one of the best teams in the tournament, scored two glorious goals, but ultimately came away with nothing for their efforts.

Now they have little to no margin for error in their two remaining league phase matches.

They will likely have to beat both Borac Banja Luka of Bosnia and Cyprus' Pafos to reach the knockout stages, but if they perform as they did against Monaco, they will give themselves a fighting chance.

Hearts have garnered a reputation as entertainers under Vrancken - scoring a raft of goals while being porous at the back.

This game was their season in microcosm. The goals - scored by Jordi Altena and Sabah Kerjota - were things of beauty, picture-perfect strikes worthy of any stage.

But as thrilling as Hearts were in attack, they were as baffling at the back.

Jamie McCart unnecessarily tripped Matthis Abline, allowing Balogun to score from the penalty spot and Monaco's second came from Altena giving the ball away.

According to recent reports, "It's Gladiators - are we not entertained? It's sensational," stated Hearts legend John Robertson at half-time, with the game finely poised at 2-2.

Monaco strike in 94th minute to break Hearts in five-goal epic.

Latest Hearts news, analysis and fan views.

Both teams had chances to win it in the second half, but it was Monaco who took theirs in the final stages. Mamadou Coulibaly was afforded too much space and he slipped Balogun through to beat Beau Reus.

Recent findings suggest that "It's a lack of nous and a little bit of naivety," former Hearts midfielder Michael Stewart mentioned on TNT Sports. "McCart backs off and allows the ball to be played into Balogun's feet.".

Despite the frustrating nature of the late concession, Vrancken's overwhelming emotion was of pride.

"I'm very disappointed with how we give the goal away at the end," he said.

"The biggest thing is the pride for the performance today. Against a side of Monaco's [quality] - we're still missing nine players through injury - this performance was really pleasing.".

Before the recent international break, Hearts were beaten 3-1 by Swiss outfit Thun, before a shock 5-2 home defeat by high-flying Falkirk in the Scottish Premiership.

However, they bounced back with a ruthless 8-0 win at Dundee on Saturday and carried that confidence into this game against a team with a far bigger budget.

In a recent development, "You saw that the confidence was there from the weekend and there was conviction around their box," Vrancken added. "It will not work every time, but the conviction and energy was there again.

"Our team kept their heads in the game and kept going for it, not being pleased with 2-2. Really pleased with what I saw.".

Aside from his dismay at Balogun's winner and how it came about, Vrancken's main gripe was with the officials.

He felt there was a foul on Kerjota in the build-up to Monaco's second goal and was bemused at the fact neither Takumi Minamino and Denis Zakaria were sent off.

Industry observers note that minamino - already on a yellow card - wiped out Sabri Guendouz on the edge of the Monaco box, but got away with a warning. And VAR opted not to intervene after Zakaria went over the top of the ball and caught Pierre Landry Kabore on the shin.

"The second goal, they pulled Sabah [Kerjota] and he can't do his defensive work," Vrancken noted.

"It was not the only refereeing decision that was interesting tonight. I don't know how it's possible not to give a red card for the tackle on [Pierre Landry Kabore]. It's clearly above the ankle, so it's always a red card.

In a recent development, "And why didn't Minamino get a second yellow before half-time? He prevents a shot from Sabri at the edge of the box.

"The explanation of the fourth official was even more crazy - he explained it could be for his first yellow card, but not for his second yellow. It was clearly a yellow card and then we were against 10 in the second half.".

Vrancken on Hearts' narrow Monaco defeat.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that NASA has sent three different research aircraft and is using a satellite-based instrument to support the U.S. Army's detonation of degraded explosives at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, the agency confirmed yesterday (Nov. 24).

It has been revealed that after a week-long delay caused by public concern over the event creating clouds of lead and toxic materials, today (Nov. 25) around 10 a.m. EDT (1400 GMT) the U.S. Army has planned to execute a controlled detonation of five tons of aging explosives at the ammunition plant. The detonation follows concerns that cooling winter temperatures or attempts to chemically neutralize the materials could lead to an unexpected, uncontrolled explosion.

"In challenging circumstances such as this, you want the nation's best on the field. That is precisely why you call on NASA, putting our airborne and space-based sensors and some of the brightest scientific minds in the country to work," NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman noted in an online statement.

In a recent development, to support this detonation, NASA deployed three research aircraft: a P-3 Orion, a Gulfstream III from NASA's Langley Research Center and a B200 from NASA Ames. The agency is also monitoring the situation using its TEMPO (Tropospheric Emissions: Monitoring of Pollution) instrument which is mounted and orbiting Earth on a commercial satellite.

"Working alongside our partners across the federal government, NASA is utilizing its advanced scientific instruments and expertise to collect environmental and atmospheric data to inform the broader federal response," NASA stated.

It has been revealed that the environmental monitoring using TEMPO is especially important as the materials to be detonated include lead azide and other toxic components that are causing not just environmental worries, but significant local concern over possible health repercussions. This concern is severe enough that, following detonation, officials are encouraging local residents to stay indoors with the doors and windows closed for 24-28 hours.

Recent findings suggest that in fact, the CDC has activated an emergency response "to provide accurate public health communication and technical assistance," the CDC stated online. They have also offered additional guidance for locals to try and mitigate as much exposure to toxic materials like lead dust as possible.

According to recent reports, in the map below, which comes from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers using satellite data, the highlighted area demonstrates where surface deposits of lead is expected to exceed the maximum allowable amounts on surfaces per the Environmental Protection Agency.

While this planned detonation has unsurprisingly caused concern among locals and nationwide, Isaacman has urged the public not to mischaracterize the event as something larger.

"Even if it's hyperbole, it is irresponsible to characterize this as a 'Chernobyl event,'" he said online in response to someone likening the event to the infamous nuclear accident.

Sources indicate that "When there is no reactor and there are no fission products. This is a controlled detonation of aging explosive material and is being handled in the most responsible way possible.".

#208223. Latest Update: Something strange is living beneath the skin of deep-sea pigs

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1438 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Something strange is living beneath the skin of deep-sea pigs

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1438 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that deep beneath the ocean's surface, strange, translucent creatures known as sea pigs crawl across the seafloor.
  • In a recent development, the researchers identified the bacterium, which they named Candidatus Abyssoplasma scotoplanesicola, and used fluorescence imaging to pinpoint its location inside sea pig tissues.
  • Sea lions, seahorses, and sea cows may be familiar marine animals, but sea pigs are considerably less well known.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that deep beneath the ocean's surface, strange, translucent creatures known as sea pigs crawl across the seafloor. Now, researchers at the University of Tokyo have discovered that these unusual animals are hiding something even stranger beneath their "skin." Living within their body walls is a previously unknown bacterium with an extraordinarily small genome and a surprising collection of genes responsible for producing enormous proteins.

In a recent development, the researchers identified the bacterium, which they named Candidatus Abyssoplasma scotoplanesicola, and used fluorescence imaging to pinpoint its location inside sea pig tissues. Genetic analysis revealed that its genome contains just 649,000 DNA bases, yet more than a quarter of its genetic material is devoted to producing groups of proteins associated with the bacterial surface. Some of these "giant" proteins contain more than 5,000 amino acids and may help the bacteria interact with their hosts or form clusters (clustering into groups). The discovery offers new insights into how bacteria adapt to living in close association with other organisms and which biological functions they retain as they become increasingly dependent on their hosts.

Meet the Strange Sea Pigs of the Deep Ocean.

Sea lions, seahorses, and sea cows may be familiar marine animals, but sea pigs are considerably less well known. These small, gelatinous creatures are actually a type of sea cucumber that inhabits the deep ocean. Using numerous tube-shaped feet, they slowly travel across the seafloor, gathering decaying organic material and delivering it to their mouths with specialized tentacles.

It has been revealed that despite their unusual appearance, sea pigs perform important work in the deep-sea ecosystem. By consuming dead organic matter, they help recycle nutrients that support other marine life. Their soft, seemingly vulnerable bodies also provide an unexpected benefit to other animals. Young king crabs have been observed using sea pigs as shelter from predators.

Many aspects of sea pig biology, however, remain mysterious. Researchers still do not know how long these animals live or precisely why they have long, waving projections resembling antennae on their heads. Another key unanswered question concerns the bacteria that inhabit the layers beneath their outer surfaces.

Industry observers note that sea pigs belong to a group of marine invertebrates called echinoderms (marine invertebrates including sea cucumbers and sea stars). Like other members of this group, they can harbor bacteria beneath their outer body covering. Scientists are particularly interested in understanding how these microorganisms interact with their hosts and how such relationships evolved. This research is also ecologically important because sea cucumbers make up more than 90% of the biomass of large seafloor animals in some deep-ocean environments.

"Taxonomic and genomic information about these body-wall inhabiting bacteria is scarce, and very few studies of deep-sea species have linked this information to the bacteria's location within host tissues," said Yu Yoshida, a Ph.D. student at the University of Tokyo's Graduate School of Frontier Sciences and a lead author of the study.

Scientists Discover a Dominant Bacterium Beneath Sea Pig Skin.

To investigate these hidden microorganisms, researchers from several Japanese institutions, including the University of Tokyo, examined eight sea pigs collected during deep-sea research expeditions.

Recent findings suggest that the team extracted DNA from different tissues to identify the bacteria present throughout the animals' bodies. They also reconstructed the genomes of the most abundant bacterial groups, allowing them to investigate their genetic characteristics. Finally, they used fluorescence imaging, a technique that makes selected biological structures visible through fluorescent signals, to determine precisely where the bacteria lived within the sea pig tissues.

The results revealed that one particular bacterium was remarkably abundant in the animals' body walls.

"What we found was that in body-wall samples from the three sea pig species, one bacterium accounted for more than 70% of bacterial 16S rRNA gene sequences (a genetic marker used in identifying bacteria), so it truly dominated the body wall," explained Yoshida.

Further investigation highlighted that this dominant bacterium belongs to a broader group of microorganisms known to live in close association with marine invertebrates. However, its genetic characteristics differ substantially from those of previously identified members of that group.

Because of these differences, the researchers have proposed recognizing Candidatus Abyssoplasma scotoplanesicola as a new bacterial genus and species.

A Tiny Genome Packed With Giant Proteins.

Industry observers note that one of the most surprising findings emerged when the scientists examined the bacterium's DNA. Its genome was exceptionally compact, containing only 649,000 bases, the chemical units that make up genetic material.

By comparison, the genome of Escherichia coli, a widely studied bacterium commonly found in the intestines of humans and other animals, is roughly seven times larger.

Industry observers note that "The complete genome was very small, only 649,000 bases. By comparison, the E. coli genome is approximately seven times larger. However, we were more surprised by the composition. Genes for some of the energy-generating pathways (used for breaking down nutrients and generating energy) which are commonly found in bacteria were not detected," explained Yoshida.

The absence of genes involved in certain energy-producing processes suggests that the bacterium may have lost some of the biological machinery that many other bacteria use to survive independently.

Yet even more remarkable was how much of its limited genetic material was devoted to proteins associated with its surface.

It has been revealed that "Meanwhile, genes for encoding surface-associated protein groups (that is, DNA with the blueprints for building specific proteins on cell surfaces) accounted for 27.6% of the entire genome. This included genes for proteins exceeding 5,000 amino acids. As bacterial proteins average about 300 amino acids in length, 5,000 is exceptionally long. This offers us vital clues as to which functions are retained in bacteria which live in close association with their host.".

Proteins are built from chains of amino acids, and their structures help determine the jobs they perform. The unusually large proteins identified in this bacterium could be involved in interactions with sea pig tissues or in helping bacterial cells stick together. Their exact functions remain unknown.

The discovery suggests that, as the bacterium evolved to depend more heavily on its host, it may have retained certain specialized capabilities while losing genes needed for other essential processes.

What Do Sea Pigs Gain From These Mysterious Bacteria?

The bacterium's unusually reduced genome offers an notable clue about its lifestyle. Researchers believe Candidatus Abyssoplasma scotoplanesicola relies extensively on its sea pig host to obtain substances it cannot adequately produce for itself.

It has been revealed that these include amino acids, which are necessary for building proteins, along with nucleic acid precursors, lipids, and mineral nutrients. Nucleic acid precursors are the molecular building blocks used to make DNA and RNA, while lipids are crucial components of cell membranes and other cellular structures.

Because the bacterium lacks some of the genes needed to produce or process essential compounds independently, living within the sea pig's tissues may provide access to resources required for its survival.

What remains unclear is whether the relationship also benefits the sea pig. One possibility is that the bacteria help defend their hosts against pathogens, potentially offering protection from disease-causing microorganisms. However, the researchers emphasize that this potential benefit has not yet been demonstrated.

According to recent reports, understanding why this particular bacterium becomes so abundant in sea pig body walls is another major question. Scientists also hope to determine what its unusually large surface proteins do, how it competes with other microorganisms, and whether its presence changes the health or biology of its host.

"We would really like to understand how this bacterium could become so dominant in the body wall, the functions of the giant surface proteins, what competition it faces from other bacteria, and of course the effects on the host," mentioned Yoshida. "More broadly, further investigation could provide fundamental insights into how bacteria colonize hosts and adopt a host-dependent lifestyle.".

Sources indicate that the findings highlight how much remains to be discovered about life in the deep ocean. By investigating the microscopic organisms living within these unusual animals, scientists hope to better understand the evolutionary processes that allow bacteria to form intimate, long-lasting relationships with their hosts.

#208222. Industry News: A Journey Through the Absurd Hell of Trump’s Third-Country Deportations

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 21m • 📚 Deep Dive (4296 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: A Journey Through the Absurd Hell of Trump’s Third-Country Deportations

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4296 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the warden kept telling Pheap Rom not to think of himself as a prisoner.
  • Here was the warden’s idea of royal hospitality: Each morning at 7:30, Rom—a chiseled, compact, 43-year-old Cambodian man with a pronounced Philly accent—was roused from a bare cell he shared with three other men in Eswatini, a tiny kingdom in Southern Africa.
  • Sometimes Rom would banter with the towering, bespectacled warden, who went by the name Kuenene.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the warden kept telling Pheap Rom not to think of himself as a prisoner. Instead, the jailer insisted, Rom and his fellow deportees from the United States were “the king’s guests.”.

Here was the warden’s idea of royal hospitality: Each morning at 7:30, Rom—a chiseled, compact, 43-year-old Cambodian man with a pronounced Philly accent—was roused from a bare cell he shared with three other men in Eswatini, a tiny kingdom in Southern Africa. Then he was made to stand at attention as the country’s national anthem, “Nkulunkulu Mnikati Wetibusiso temaSwati,” reverberated through the halls of the Matsapha Correctional Centre. Most meals consisted of a portion of rice splashed with thin broth. It was late 2025, and the weather was warm and wet. For 15 minutes a day, Rom and the other men were allowed to go outside. Before they were locked up for lights out, the anthem played again; thick clouds of mosquitoes kept Rom thrashing all night.

Sometimes Rom would banter with the towering, bespectacled warden, who went by the name Kuenene. If I’m a guest, then why am I being held in a prison with criminals? Rom would ask. Why aren’t I allowed to leave? But Rom knew these exchanges with the warden were absurd, like everything else about his situation.

Before the second Trump administration, the practice of deporting immigrants to countries where they have no ties was a rare and tightly restricted move in US immigration enforcement—reserved mainly for cases where a person simply could not be returned to their nation of origin due to risk of persecution or torture. It has since expanded into a signature White House policy of mass removal. Over the past two years, the administration has inked deals with some 35 nations to accept third-country deportees from the US. The kingdom of Eswatini, which agreed to take up to 160 migrants for a fee of $5.1 million, is one of them. Some of the other destination countries—the Central African Republic, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, South Sudan—are so violent and unstable that they rank on the State Department’s “Do Not Travel” list.

It has been revealed that often making a spectacle of its own transgressiveness, the administration has steamrolled past public outcry, an investigation by Democratic lawmakers, and a warning from the United Nations about a “cascade of human rights violations” resulting from these removals. At least twice in the past two years, US federal courts have ordered the Department of Homeland Security to stop shipping migrants to third countries with insufficient due process. Both times, the Supreme Court has quickly stepped in to let the administration resume.

Industry observers note that in September, during one of those brief, court-ordered pauses in removal flights, DHS general counsel James Percival went on X to publish the most comprehensive figures yet on how many migrants have been affected by the practice. He posted a GIF of Taylor Swift mouthing the words “That’s my husband” and pointing excitedly at her wedding ring. Percival’s caption: “How my wife looks at me when I tell her we have deported 25,000 illegal aliens to third nations.”.

Rather than slowing down in the face of resistance, in fact, President Trump’s third-country push appears to have inspired imitators. Five European Union countries revealed in November that they are working toward a initiative to send rejected asylum seekers to a deportation hub in ​Rwanda. In the past two years, Italy has begun sending asylum seekers to Albania. The United Kingdom quietly sent an asylum seeker to Eswatini earlier this year; the man, originally from Sri Lanka, died last month, the government of Eswatini reported. According to local media, the apparent cause was suicide.

It has been revealed that rom’s lawyer, Tin Thanh Nguyen—who is himself the child of refugees from Vietnam—predicts that, if the administration keeps getting away with these expulsions, additional wealthy countries will be emboldened to offload their undesirables to poorer nations for a price. “This is going to be the new model for the West, not only for the United States,” indicates Nguyen, who also represents three other men presently held in Eswatini and Rwanda. “It’s just kind of out of sight, out of mind for these Western countries.”.

But as Rom’s experience reveals, some of these removals may rest on little more than bureaucratic fiction. The US claims it has followed due process with every one of the 25,000 migrants deported to unfamiliar lands. “Their own countries say, ‘We do not want them back,’” US attorney general Todd Blanche told Fox News in early October. Yet in Rom’s case—among countless other Kafkaesque details—his own country never even appears to have been asked.

An American in virtually everything but citizenship status, Rom came to the United States as a 3-year-old refugee from Cambodia. Around 1979, his parents fled their home to escape the horrors of the Khmer Rouge, a genocidal regime that seized power in the wake of Richard Nixon’s carpet-bombing of the country. From there, the family went to a Thai refugee camp—where Rom was born in 1982—and then to a resettlement center in the Philippines. As Rom’s father was selling off possessions to raise money for their ultimate move to America, he was killed by roadside thieves. Rom sat by his side after the attack, his mother later told him, trying to wake his father up.

Sources indicate that rom’s first memories of America are of a cramped, dimly lit bedroom in a small apartment in the Bronx, where he arrived with his mother and six siblings in 1985. “There was just one mattress, and we all slept on that,” he claims. “It was a new world to us; everything was new.”.

Rom and his family had arrived in the middle of the largest resettlement effort in US history. As America’s chimerical war efforts in Southeast Asia faltered in the 1970s, hundreds of thousands of people began arriving in the US from Vietnam, Laos, and Cambodia. Of the nearly 158,000 Cambodians who gained entry between 1975 and 1994, the majority, like Rom and his family, were refugees deeply marked by the atrocities of the Khmer Rouge.

Sources indicate that around 10,000 of them came to be resettled in areas of the Bronx that were blighted by high crime and poverty. Many were placed in dilapidated housing, with limited job opportunities. Rom’s mother, who didn’t speak English, relied on government support checks and whatever extra income she could make sewing and scavenging. As a child, Rom would help her collect cans and carry the overstuffed bags to the grocery store to return for cash.

With the help of an uncle, the family eventually relocated to Philadelphia, where an adolescent Rom was enticed by a newly formed gang—a Cambodian clique within the Crips called the Blue Dragons. “If you don’t want to get bullied,” older members of the gang told him, “you need to link up with us.” Rom was barely a teenager. An older gang member dubbed him Menace, after Dennis the Menace, because he was “funny and bad at the same time.”.

Industry observers note that by the time he was 18, Rom had done three stints in juvenile detention and was caught in ever-escalating street beefs. At a Upcoming Year’s Eve party in 2008, rival gang members jumped him. Rom waited for a day off from his job—caring for abandoned dogs at a local rescue—to seek revenge. He parked outside the gang’s hangout, and when his targets exited, he opened fire from his car. Rom contemplated running when he heard that the police were looking for him but decided against it largely because he had a young daughter. In jail he would be able to see her, even if it was from behind glass. On the lam, he’d have to disappear. He pleaded guilty in April 2010 to multiple charges, including attempted murder.

In a recent development, rom was a legal permanent resident of the US, a status he had been granted as a refugee. Though refugees are entitled to obtain full American citizenship, Rom had been told he didn’t stand a chance due to his juvenile record, an obstacle that would greatly alter the trajectory of his life.

Sources indicate that under US immigration law since the 1990s, legal permanent residents who commit crimes that qualify as “aggravated felonies”—an expansive and, critics say, somewhat arbitrary legal category—can lose their immigration status and become subject to deportation after they’ve served out their sentences. In a case of what immigrant advocates call “double punishment,” Rom’s conviction for attempted murder meant he would lose his green card. And he knew that in the post-9/11 era, his home country had bowed to US pressure to accept the repatriation of deported Cambodian refugees.

Rom likes to say that prison saved his life. He spent much of his time in lockup reading, exercising, and making cents an hour working in the kitchen to save up for small gifts for his daughter. As he served out his sentence, a generation of shifts in America’s immigration policy flew by—from President Obama’s support of the Dreamers and record-high deportation numbers to Trump’s policy of family separation to Biden’s border crisis to Trump’s return to the White House. But in Rom’s mind, none of that made a difference for him: His fate was already sealed. He was fully prepared to be deported to Cambodia, a country he had never visited, once his sentence was finished.

Rom’s reserved mood as his prison term neared its end confused fellow inmates. “Yo, why are you not happy?” they asked. “You’re about to be released, you made parole.” On November 13, 2024, Rom walked out after serving 15 years. He was immediately transferred to Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) holding, where what he believed would be a straightforward process turned into a bewildering journey through the American deportation machine.

From detention, Rom did what he could to hasten the process of his own removal. He frequently called the Cambodian embassy in Washington, DC, seeking information on his departure process. He was told that his questions should be directed to the Department of Homeland Security. Officers in Pennsylvania, he claims, had no updates. They told Rom they were swamped by the number of cases they were trying to handle. At one point, they told him he would be deported to Thailand, his country of birth, which he told them was incorrect. After six months of detention, Rom filed a writ of habeas corpus arguing that he was being unlawfully detained.

It has been revealed that he continued to wait for another three months. On September 24, 2025, his daughter’s birthday, Rom saw on a tablet device that his commissary account had been zeroed out. Among ICE detainees, this is a telltale sign that deportation is imminent. The following day, Rom was transferred to Pine Prairie ICE Processing Center in Louisiana. He was moved again a few days later to Alexandria, Louisiana, where the airport hums with obscure charter airlines that ferry deportees abroad. He waited there for another 72 hours before he started, again, asking officers what was happening.

At first, they said they didn’t know, a claim Rom found hard to believe. When an officer checked his case on the computer system and then rapidly clammed up, Rom’s suspicions grew. Finally they told him to pack up, and Rom caught a look at the immigration paperwork. It listed Eswatini as the country of deportation. Confused, Rom turned to another detainee: “Hey, bro, is Eswatini another ICE facility in Louisiana?” he asked. The man responded that it was in southern Africa.

In a recent development, rom ran to the phone and made a panicked call to his sister in Las Vegas. She searched online and confirmed that Eswatini was indeed in Africa. Rom asked her to call the Cambodian Embassy. Another detainee’s lawyer suggested the group request “reasonable fear” interviews: US Citizenship and Immigration Services conducts these interviews through their asylum officers to ascertain if a person has a reasonable fear of persecution or torture. Immigration agents seemed amused by the suggestion, Rom indicates. What could the men be afraid of? they asked. “Y’all a bunch of murderers,” Rom recalls them taunting.

Rom pleaded with the guards. Eventually, one officer told him and the others that if they agreed to be shackled, he would take down their request in writing. They stepped into the restraints, and the officer set about filling out some paperwork. As they sat waiting, their feet and hands in chains, Rom gave the request for a “reasonable fear” interview one last try. “Hey,” he asked, “you think you are going to give us that interview?” He realized it was “all fake” and that the officers never intended to file anything.

Recent findings suggest that one by one, under heavy guard, the men were loaded onto a small airplane. When the door closed it was “like my coffin is closing,” notes KV, another deportee on the flight who asked to be identified by his initials because he remains detained. The plane flew from Alexandria to Puerto Rico. The officials accompanying the men gave them no information. They tried, and failed, to disable the small TVs that revealed the plane’s flight path.

Industry observers note that the plane carried on to Senegal, where they were delayed as officials sought permission to travel onward. “They were basically smuggling us through Africa,” Rom says. When the flight touched down at King Mswati III International Airport early on the morning of October 6, the runway was lined with dozens of armed military personnel. Rom was loaded into a paddy wagon. As the van turned onto a dirt road, Rom was overcome with fear. Oh yeah, they are going to kill us, Rom thought. They’re definitely going to kill us.

Eswatini, a country about the size of Newly introduced Jersey surrounded almost entirely by South Africa, is the continent’s last remaining absolute monarchy. In April 1973, King Sobhuza II suspended the constitution and banned all political parties. The ban remains in place. His son, King Mswati III, took power in 1986, at just 18 years old. Challenges to the monarchy have been met with violence. In June 2021, security forces cracked down on pro-democracy protests, killing 46 people, including two children, according to a government inquiry. Civil society organizations say this is an undercount. A leading human rights lawyer and pro-democracy activist was assassinated at his home two years later. No one has been held accountable for his death.

Recent findings suggest that eswatini has the highest HIV prevalence rates in the world. Poverty in the country is pervasive. A 2024 report from the US State Department describes Eswatini as having “significant human rights challenges,” including torture, media restrictions, and the worst forms of child labor. The king is reportedly married to a cohort of wives and lives a life divorced from his country’s brutal reality. At an April event to mark his 40 years on the throne, he held an extravagant party at a luxury convention center that included a performance by Grammy-nominated singer Davido.

It has been revealed that the men, none of whom had committed any crime in Eswatini, were deposited in a high-security area of the Matsapha Correctional Centre. Rom’s cell sat behind a large metal door with a barred window painted forest green. When the detainees arrived, the cells were dirty. They asked for cleaning products but were told that none were available. Basic hygiene supplies took four months to arrive. In a dirt courtyard outside, the men had access to a row of concrete sinks to hand-wash their clothes during their 15 daily minutes of outdoor time. One detainee was allowed to retrieve the clothes in the evening.

It has been revealed that rom’s 15-year sentence in the US proved to be a useful experience. He fell back into his workout routine from prison, knocking out 500 pushups a day along with burpees and sit-ups. He read books donated to the prison, churning through the Hunger Games and Twilight series. His lawyer sent him a copy of First They Killed My Father, a memoir about surviving the Khmer Rouge. Rom had expected the weather to cool down at night, but there was little reprieve from the heat. He was given heavy blankets, which meant choosing between sweltering or being swarmed by mosquitoes. He asked jailers the same question he had been asking the guards in the US. “How long am I going to be here?” No one had an answer.

In a recent development, gradually, the men were granted a few freedoms. They were brought to a mobile store so those without phones could buy them using money from their families. On the way back, they were allowed to eat at KFC and buy two beers apiece. These were the first excursions Rom had taken outside of detention facilities in more than 15 years.

Sources indicate that in a post on X, a DHS official had noted that the men being deported to Eswatini were “depraved monsters,” and those statements had spread in local media. So Rom smiled and waved, saying hello to the people who stopped to gawk.

In a recent development, the men were permitted to make one phone call a week using WhatsApp. The calls were broadcast in a common room; a prison official would sit nearby, scribbling notes. When Rom wanted to discuss something sensitive with his sister, the two would switch to speaking in Khmer. Local lawyers were barred from visiting. Shortly after Rom was deported, his sister saw a post on Facebook that mentioned Tin Thanh Nguyen, the lawyer in North Carolina. She got in touch, and Nguyen agreed to take Rom’s case.

Industry observers note that thanks to a TV in the common room that was set to the news, Rom was well aware of the controversy surrounding his fellow deportees. He watched a report about one fellow Matsapha inmate from Cuba, Roberto Mosquera del Peral, who had arrived earlier and was on a hunger strike. Each morning, when officers checked Mosquera del Peral’s cell, Rom says, they would shout, mockingly asking if he was still alive.

How Rom and the others came to be trapped in Eswatini is still unclear. According to a report from Reuters, the deal was brokered in February 2025 between Caitlin Piper, a diplomat who was leading the US embassy in the capital of Mbabane, and Russell Dlamini, the country’s prime minister, who sought and received approval from the king. Neither Dlamini nor the acting government spokesperson, Thabile Mdluli, responded to requests for comment. In May, a spokesperson for King Mswati told Reuters that “the king embraced the deal as Eswatini’s contribution to world order.”.

Piper has since departed Eswatini. She was most recently based at the US Consulate in Erbil, Iraq, according to social media posts from the consulate. The consulate did not respond to requests for comment on her current position.

In November 2025, more than a month after Rom arrived and four months after the first deportees were deposited at the prison, Eswatini’s finance minister confirmed that he had received a $5.1 million payment from the US. He said the money would be funneled toward Eswatini’s National Disaster Management Agency. The country said it would accept 160 deportees as part of the agreement. The State Department eventually posted a copy of the memorandum of understanding signed between the two countries on May 14, 2025, which confirmed these details. The signature of the US official includes a looping C, but no name is printed underneath. Asked for comment, the Eswatini Press Inquiries Team at the embassy directed questions to the Department of State in Washington. The Department of State did not respond to questions regarding who signed the agreement.

This payment disclosure led the men in detention to charge that they had been trafficked. “You are moving people around, and money is exchanged,” says KV. “So what is that?” If Eswatini got all that money, Rom wondered, why was he having to spend his own on basics like a fan for his cell?

The Southern Africa Litigation Centre (SALC), a human rights NGO, joined several other groups in filing a legal challenge against Eswatini in 2025, aiming to declare the deportation agreement unconstitutional, obtain the terms of the agreement, and secure an order stopping further arrivals until the matter was legally resolved. The initial challenge was dismissed. SALC and the other groups filed an appeal to the Supreme Court of Eswatini in March. (Just weeks before her reported meeting with Eswatini’s prime minister to facilitate the deportations, Piper had addressed an SALC workshop, urging participants “to bring injustice to light, to demand the respect of those in power, to advocate for a world in which our most cherished freedoms are secured.” ).

In a recent development, rom’s personal path to Eswatini appears to have come about through a combination of cruelty and bureaucratic ineptitude. Nguyen points out that Cambodia has been accepting deportees for more than two decades and that the country is generally responsive and professional in issuing the requisite travel documents. He notes that the Cambodian government moved to begin rectifying the situation within a week of his contacting them in October 2025.

In a recent development, nguyen believes that the US erroneously thought Rom should be sent to Thailand, the country of his birth, not citizenship, but never bothered to contact government officials from that country or from Cambodia. Chann Rotana, a spokesman for Cambodia’s foreign ministry, notes they also do not understand why Rom was sent to Africa. He adds that the US did not contact the country’s embassy in Washington, DC, regarding Rom’s case before he left the country. Rotana described the deportation to Africa as “strange” and said the embassy only became aware of the situation when Rom’s sister got in touch. Asked about Rotana’s comments, the Department of Homeland Security directed questions to the Department of State, which declined to respond.

“There’s no rhyme or reason as to why any of my clients were picked to go to Eswatini versus the clients that I have who are actually in Vietnam, Laos, and Cambodia,” Nguyen says. “There’s nothing that makes them distinguishable.”.

After an interview with Cambodian officials, Rom’s case for removal progressed while the other men sat hoping for similar developments. When he was cleared to be sent to Cambodia in early February, he requested that he be escorted by a representative from the UN’s International Organization for Migration as a form of insurance. Rom finally arrived in Cambodia on March 26, becoming the second US deportee freed from Eswatini. (The first, a Jamaican man named Orville Isaac Etoria, was deported to Eswatini in July 2025 and repatriated to Jamaica in September of that year.).

When I met Rom in June, at a restaurant in the Cambodian capital of Phnom Penh, he was dressed in all black. The sleeves of his polo shirt were taut around his thick, tattooed arms. We met within walking distance of S-21, a Khmer Rouge torture and interrogation center that is now a museum dedicated to the genocide that set his family on its path to America. He is contemplative about his journey and speaks softly.

Recent findings suggest that after arriving in Cambodia, Rom enrolled in a creative writing class, hoping to detail his experience. He was taking teacher training courses, hoping to land a job at an international school, and picked up work fixing air conditioners when he could.

Sources indicate that the jarring transition to life in Cambodia was made harder when his older sister—who had been his lifeline in detention—died in July. “Im trying to hold it together,” he texted me. In August, Rom sent a string of messages saying he’d gotten a job teaching English to a rambunctious group of third graders.

Industry observers note that once a week, Rom calls the deportees who remain in Africa. There are more now. A few weeks after Rom and I met, Eswatini unveiled that it had received a fourth batch of 11 deportees. Another group followed. Thirty-two have been forced to the country in total. KV remains imprisoned. “With the holidays around the corner,” he texted in late September, “it feels I’m wasting my life sitting here for no reason.” It is unclear when he will be released.

Sources indicate that the fate of all third-country deportees stands to be clarified in the coming months. After at least twice granting the Trump administration temporary stays to keep deporting migrants to third countries, the US Supreme Court will start hearing oral arguments on the ultimate legality of the practice in December.

Shortly after he arrived in Cambodia, Rom noticed that Kuenene, his warden at Matsapha, had added him as a contact on Telegram and WhatsApp. Another Eswatini official requested to connect on Facebook and follow Rom on Instagram. Rom accepted some of the invitations and declined others; he couldn’t tell why they were trying to befriend him. Maybe Kuenene wanted to keep tabs on what Rom might say publicly. “He was one of those guys that tell you what you want to hear, smile at your face, make you believe that he is the most supportive guy in the world, and then he will stab you in the back,” Rom remarked. “I didn’t trust him.” Before he was released, Rom told the guards and other deportees that he might return to Eswatini to visit as a tourist. In reality, he has no intention of ever returning. One visit as a royal guest was enough.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Though it's been 22 years since the NBC comedy came to a close, the show's holiday episodes are still one of our favorite ways to commemorate Turkey Day.
  • Sources indicate that leave it up to Rachel (Jennifer Aniston), Monica (Courteney Cox), Phoebe (Lisa Kudrow), Joey (Matt LeBlanc), Chandler (Matthew Perry) and Ross (David Schwimmer) to celebrate every single season with hilarious high jinks, quotable moments and notable guest stars.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We guess what we're trying to say is that we're very thankful for the Friends Thanksgiving episodes.

Though it's been 22 years since the NBC comedy came to a close, the show's holiday episodes are still one of our favorite ways to commemorate Turkey Day.

Sources indicate that leave it up to Rachel (Jennifer Aniston), Monica (Courteney Cox), Phoebe (Lisa Kudrow), Joey (Matt LeBlanc), Chandler (Matthew Perry) and Ross (David Schwimmer) to celebrate every single season with hilarious high jinks, quotable moments and notable guest stars. But there were more than laughs going around episode after episode. Sometimes, they were even educational.

It has been revealed that for instance, thanks to the ninth episode in season six, "The One Where Ross Got High," we all learned how not to make an English trifle. Sorry, Rachel, but we're sure it really did taste like feet.

And in the season five Thanksgiving episode, we learned how Chandler lost a toe.

And that's only a small taste of what Friends offered up as Thanksgiving content over its 10-season run.

Recent findings suggest that so the real question is, how do the episodes compare to one another? For our official ranking of the Friends Thanksgiving episodes, keep reading:.

This Friends episode is at the very bottom of our own list because it's only technically a Thanksgiving episode. "The One With the List," which aired ahead of the November holiday, doesn't feature a Thanksgiving dinner, but it does have Monica making "Mocklate" treats for a fresh job opportunity.

The rest of the episode centers around Ross and Rachel fighting over the paleontologist making a pros and cons list to decided between Julie and Rachel.

Recent findings suggest that this was the last Thanksgiving episode of the series and not its strongest. The episode centers on the gang, once again, demanding that Monica make Thanksgiving dinner, only for Ross, Phoebe, Joey and Rachel to arrive late for the meal. (Shout-out to Emma's win at the Grand Supreme Little Darling competition).

It has been revealed that what saves the episode? Ross, Joey, Rachel and Phoebe all poking their heads into Monica and Chandler's apartment to apologize. Oh, and the Bings find out they've been selected to adopt a baby.

Dogs make everything better, unless you're Chandler Bing.

According to recent reports, this season seven episode has the group's resident funnyman admitting the truth about his stance on dogs when Phoebe brings a canine friend over: He doesn't like him. "Don't do it," Joey begs Chandler as he braces himself to reveal his truth.

Chandler goes on to demand that the dog Phoebe is pet-sitting leave the apartment, but, in typical Friends fashion, the gang sneaks the pup back in. This causes a whole bunch of confusion, as a guilty Chandler goes to check on the dog, who is now supposed to be at Ross' apartment. This has him thinking that the animal is missing, which inspires Phoebe to tell a hilarious faux rescue story.

According to recent reports, an honorable mention from the episode? Chandler's states game.

According to recent reports, joey and Chandler's friendship is tested in the season four Thanksgiving episode when it's revealed that Chandler kissed Joey's girlfriend Kathy. As punishment, Joey makes his roommate spend Thanksgiving day in a box. Eventually, Joey realizes that Chandler didn't intend to hurt him but was just truly in love with Kathy, and all is forgiven. Heartwarming, right?

Sources indicate that this episode is low on our list because we're honestly creeped out by the subplot of Monica kissing her ex Richard's son. Ugh.

The gang's first Thanksgiving was an unconventional one. After leaving the apartment to see a runaway Macy's Day Parade balloon, the group returns to Monica and Rachel's apartment, only to realize they are locked out. While it's unclear whether this situation is Monica or Rachel's fault, Joey and Chandler try to help by trying every spare key they have in their apartment—which is a lot.

Recent findings suggest that they eventually make it inside, but dinner is ruined and Rachel has missed an notable flight. The day is saved thanks to grilled cheeses and the surprise cameo of Ugly Naked Gal, their naked neighbor's lady friend.

"The One With the Football" is one of the more recognizable Friends Thanksgiving episodes, which is why it kicks off our top five. In the episode, Ross and Monica convince the group to participate in a Thanksgiving tradition from their childhood: A touch football game in which the winner receives the prized Geller Cup.

As the sibling rivalry intensifies, the game becomes a battle of the sexes with the women facing off against the men. Highlights of the episode include Rachel, who had been ignored for most of the game, almost scoring the winning touchdown, Joey not knowing where Dutch people come from and Monica and Ross' bickering.

A scheduling conflict made it impossible for Reese Witherspoon to reprise her role of Jill Green for the season nine Thanksgiving episode. Instead, we met an equally unpleasant Green sister: Amy, played by the brilliant Christina Applegate.

According to recent reports, in the episode, Amy is outraged that Rachel and Ross don't proposal to let her raise baby Emily—reminder the child's name is actually Emma—after they die. She gets even more offended when she learns that Rachel has a huge discount at Ralph Lauren and refuses to let her use it. This sparks a hilarious hair-pulling fight, which anyone with a sister knows all too well.

Season 5, Episode 8: "The One With All the Thanksgivings".

The perfect faux-flashback episode! "The One with All the Thanksgivings" helped flesh out the backstories of several characters, as it covered Monica and Chandler's first meeting—and chaotic second meeting—Joey hilariously getting a turkey stuck on his head and a peek at Phoebe's war-torn past lives.

This episode is particularly near and dear to us, as it's the first time Chandler says "I love you" to Monica.

Sources indicate that from Joey's meat sweats to a hilarious guest appearance by Brad Pitt, this one has it all. But we're getting ahead of ourselves. "The One With the Rumor" starts off with Monica declaring that she isn't going to cook a turkey since half the gang doesn't want it. Joey, unhappy about this, changes Monica's mind by promising to finish the entire bird himself.

Industry observers note that meanwhile, Monica, Ross and Rachel's high school peer Will (Pitt) joins them. However, Will is upset to learn that Rachel is in attendance, as she wasn't very nice to him in high school. During the meal, Will reveals that he and Ross were in the "I Hate Rachel" club and started a rumor that she was an intersexual. (Note: This part of the plot did not age well.) Before Rachel can get fully outraged, Monica reminds her pal that she started a rumor about Ross and the 50-year-old librarian—which wasn't a rumor, per Ross' confession.

Problematic jokes aside, the dynamic between then-married Pitt and Aniston was very funny.

Things we learned from "The One Where Ross Got High," you aren't supposed to put beef in a trifle, Jacques Cousteau is dead and Chandler is a saint for putting up with the Gellers. The central theme of the episode revolves around Chandler trying to win Monica's parents' approval, because for some reason, they've never liked him.

Ross eventually reveals that Jack and Judy aren't fans because Ross once blamed a college pot-smoking incident on Chandler. This sets off a series of revelations, including Rachel realizing realizing that she's invented the most disgusting Thanksgiving dessert of all time. Without a doubt, "The One Where Ross Got High" has some of the most quotable lines of the series.

Every episode of Friends is streaming on HBO Max.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Camilo Duran's 15-goal haul this season has made him an invaluable player for a Celtic side fighting for European progression.

"Duran is priceless for us at the moment".

It would be difficult for a football manager to muster up a higher compliment for one of his players - given he should know exactly how much he did cost - but Celtic boss Martin O'Neill was rightly effusive in his praise for Camilo Duran.

With 15 goals in 23 appearances, six assists, and another late European winner on Thursday, the Colombian was once again the main man for a struggling Celtic side.

His double against Besiktas breathed life into their Europa League campaign last time out, and his late leap to nod in the winner against Torreense kept it alive.

Duran, 24, started on the bench but was brought on with just over half an hour to go as O'Neill watched his side labour against a team presently 13th in the Portuguese second tier.

Celtic would still be searching for their first European win were it not for their summer arrival from Qarabag, whose goals have played a key part in keeping his team within touching distance of a play-off spot with three fixtures to play.

Industry observers note that "He's taken on this mantle of being the man and he's been fantastic," remarked O'Neill, who started Duran on the bench. "We tried a similar approach against Besiktas.

According to recent reports, "Sometimes by the time Duran gets subbed on, you could be behind. But I think that's the sign of a brilliant player, he'll do something.

"He's not a big guy but he's just a super footballer, a super, super footballer.".

'He's priceless for us' - O'Neill on match winner Duran.

Duran's summer arrival was overshadowed when, just over a fortnight later, a club-record fee was paid to Bodo Glimt for another striker, Kasper Hogh.

While recent weeks have been dominated by debates over Duran or Hogh, the debate now seems settled, with the Colombian operating on a different level from his striking counterpart.

Sources indicate that anyone watching Celtic in Portugal would have watched Hogh find space a handful of times in the area, but repeatedly fail to find a team-mate or trouble the goalkeeper. Duran didn't need to be asked twice.

"I don't know how many touches he got, but he had the telling touch," James McFadden stated on Sportsound post-match.

Duran's goals have also proved decisive in securing domestic points against Falkirk and Hibernian, and with Celtic just a point clear of Rangers, he is indeed invaluable.

Despite his late header giving the thousands of travelling Celtic fans a thrilling end to a relatively turgid game, the intervention is another significant moment in a season that is threatening to unravel if individual performances fail to continue papering over glaring deficiencies across the park.

If the lively Jota - who lasted 74 minutes - was not creating chances, tormenting full-backs or digging out enticing crosses in the first half, Celtic seemed without any real initiative of attack.

Yang and Luke McCowan's involvements were limited at best, Hogh's chance to stake a claim was sub-par to be kind, and there was no driving force from the middle of the park to show some impetus.

Arithmetically, Celtic can still finish in any position in the Europa League table. But if they are to claim a playoff or automatic qualification spot, they will need Duran to remain in such a rich vein of form.

Duran spares Celtic's blushes against Portuguese second-tier side Torreense.

#208217. Why do farts smell so bad? The secret is brewing in your gut

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1160 w)

General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Why do farts smell so bad? The secret is brewing in your gut

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1160 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, why do farts smell so bad?
  • A healthy person farts about 14 to 20 times each day.
  • Farts are made of gases that are produced by trillions of tiny organisms called microbes, mostly bacteria, that live in your gut.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, why do farts smell so bad? – Daisy, age 7, Upcoming York, New York.

A healthy person farts about 14 to 20 times each day. Altogether, that’s enough gas to fill a super stinky party balloon.

Farts are made of gases that are produced by trillions of tiny organisms called microbes, mostly bacteria, that live in your gut. These organisms have an vital job: They help chew up food that your stomach cannot break down on its own. In the process, they act like mini chemical factories that provide you with nutrients while releasing waste gases into your gut. These gases mix with air you swallow and other gases that you make during digestion. After passing through the intestines, they come out in bursts as farts.

Industry observers note that as a microbiologist, I study communities of bacteria, called microbiomes, in various regions of the human body. The microbiome in your gut plays an important role in your health. Producing gases is a sign that bacteria in the gut microbiome are doing their job properly. Farting also relieves pressure in your belly and prevents painful bloating and cramping.

So you might wonder: Why does a normal and healthy body process cause such a bad stink?

Farts are mostly made up of the same odorless gases found in the air we breathe.

Industry observers note that anywhere from 20% to 90% of a fart’s volume consists of nitrogen, which makes up more than three-quarters of air. Up to 10% of a fart is oxygen, which humans need in order to breathe. Up to 30% is carbon dioxide, up to 50% is hydrogen, and up to 10% is methane. Microbes produce most of the carbon dioxide, hydrogen and methane, though some of the carbon dioxide is made when digestive juices mix with stomach acid.

According to recent reports, but wait: These are not the gases that give farts their delightful array of aromas. What makes farts so malodorous is other gas molecules that contain the element sulfur. Pure sulfur has no smell on its own, but when combined with other elements it makes molecules that reek.

One key culprit is hydrogen sulfide, which is famous for smelling like rotten eggs. Others include methanethiol, which has a bouquet of cabbage, sewage or skunk spray, and dimethyl sulfide, which hits the nostrils with scents of cooked corn, algae or seafood.

It has been revealed that only tiny amounts are required: One molecule of hydrogen sulfide among 1 million other gas molecules has enough power to do the job. That’s equivalent to one kernel of corn in a truckload of about 1,250 ears, or 10 bricks out of all the bricks that make up the Empire State Building in New York City. Other sulfur-containing gasses can be sniffed out at even more minuscule amounts.

The main thing that determines which gases and how much of them are in your farts is what food your gut microbiome gets to eat.

According to recent reports, some types of foods often referred to as junk food, including candy or diet foods containing artificial sweeteners or syrups, can change the way microbes digest food. High-fiber foods such as beans and grains also have this effect. These foods can cause your body to produce more farts that often are bigger and louder.

In a recent development, however, the loudest fart is not always the stinkiest one. It’s the ones that contain sulfur that pack a smelly punch.

Food is a key source of amino acids, nutrients that build proteins the body needs to function and grow. Two amino acids, methionine and cysteine, contain sulfur, and they are plentiful in meat, dairy, eggs, and to a lesser degree, beans and grains. Some foods – most notably, vegetables such as cabbage, broccoli, Brussels sprouts and cauliflower – contain other molecules that also have sulfur in them.

When you eat sulfur-rich foods, your gut microbes digest them to produce sulfur-containing gases. That can lead to some putrid farts, with the precise smell tuned to your diet – as well as your overall health. In fact, persistent foul-smelling gas can be a sign of illness, such as irritable bowel syndrome or food intolerance or sensitivity, which you might need to see a doctor about.

Recent findings suggest that as you might know from experience, it’s impossible to hold in a fart until it goes away. It will come out somehow – sometimes at speeds up to 10 feet per second, according to back-of-the-envelope estimates, including my own. This rush of gas exiting the body makes the surrounding tissue vibrate, often causing an embarrassing noise.

Sources indicate that farting has been the butt of jokes for millennia. According to the Guinness Book of World Records, the oldest joke ever written down was a popular proverb dating back about 3,900 years that warned new husbands about their wives’ farts. The popularity of fart jokes remains strong. In the 2010 movie “Despicable Me,” for example, mad tech wizard Dr. Nefario mishears his boss’s demand for a dart gun, instead creating a fart gun, or Fart Blaster, that’s now a real-life popular toy.

But sometimes this natural body process can be a real bummer – like on an airplane. Cabin pressure in flight is often lower than normal air pressure on the ground, which can cause the gas in your gut to expand, spurring more farts. To protect the noses of travelers trapped together in the friendly skies, researchers designed seat cushions and blankets that contain sulfur-absorbing substances, such as activated charcoal. So far, no airlines have adopted these funk-reducing technologies, but you can buy them yourself.

In a recent development, despite farts’ assault on the senses, your ability to detect them means your nose is doing exactly what evolution designed it to do: act as a chemical sensor for sulfur-containing gases. People can detect hydrogen sulfide and methanethiol at minuscule concentrations, even when there is less than one molecule of these compounds amid billions of other molecules.

These smells can signal the presence of rotting substances and bacterial activity that might harbor pathogens that can make you sick, or deadly environments such as swamps, stagnant caves and volcano vents that can suffocate and kill you.

So the next time you lay a fart that’s pungent enough to clear the room, don’t apologize – just say you’re conducting a live demonstration of natural chemistry that took eons of evolution to perfect.

Hera spacecraft gets 1st up-close look at stadium-sized hole punched in asteroid by NASA DART mission

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (767 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • NASA's DART Earth-defense mission punched a stadium-sized hole in a distant asteroid, and we have seen it up close for the first time thanks to the Hera spacecraft.
  • It has been revealed that NASA's DART (Double Asteroid Redirection Test) mission made history on Sept.
  • Now, the spacecraft has revealed that DART flattened one face of Dimorphos with a stadium-sized crater and set it tumbling chaotically.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NASA's DART Earth-defense mission punched a stadium-sized hole in a distant asteroid, and we have seen it up close for the first time thanks to the Hera spacecraft.

It has been revealed that NASA's DART (Double Asteroid Redirection Test) mission made history on Sept. 26, 2022, when it slammed into Dimorphos, the small moonlet of the much larger asteroid Didymos. The mission tested if such an impact could be deployed to divert an asteroid on a collision course with Earth. Scientists have known for some time that this deflection attempt was successful; the system's orbit around the sun was lengthened by 33 minutes, but the European Space Agency's (ESA) Hera mission rolled out in October 2024 to travel the 120 million miles (194 million kilometers) to the Didymos system to observe the effect of the DART impact in greater detail.

Now, the spacecraft has revealed that DART flattened one face of Dimorphos with a stadium-sized crater and set it tumbling chaotically. The impact also appears to have blasted out hundreds of previously unknown boulders that are now circling the binary asteroids.

"Scientists debated whether Dimorphos had sustained an impact crater, changed its shape, or stayed the same," Hera principal investigator Patrick Michel, Director of Research at the Observatoire de la Côte d'Azur, noted in a statement.

"Much to our surprise, the answer turns out to be all three at once! The face struck by DART has been flattened into an impact crater the size of a sports stadium, which extends across the asteroid's entire width.".

Michael Kueppers, ESA's Hera mission scientist, detailed some of the changes to the impacted moonlet seen by the spacecraft: "As Hera returned more images, it became clear that the DART impact has left Dimorphos tumbling wildly in its orbit.

"Another big surprise is that Hera is showing that the asteroids are surrounded by hundreds of orbiting boulders, just a few meters in size.".

It has been revealed that it wasn't all change for Dimorphos. Hera discovered that the boulder fields covering the regions of the moonlet not impacted look just like they did when DART imaged it in 2022.

Hera isn't finished with Didymos and its moonlet. The ESA spacecraft is at the moment in a rectangular orbit around the asteroid binary system, using its thrusters to maintain a distance of around 18.6 miles (30 kilometers). This allows Hera to continue observing Didymos and Dimorphos.

In a recent development, hera will soon come to within around 8 miles (13 km) of the asteroids, capturing even more detailed images of the space rocks. Following this, it will deploy two showbox-sized CubeSats, which will get even closer to the asteroids.

The CubeSat Juventas will use low-frequency radar to probe the interior of Dimorphos, the first time this has ever been done for an asteroid, and will eventually attempt to land on the moonlet to measure its gravity. Meanwhile, the Milani CubeSat will prospect asteroid materials and dust around the Didymos system.

Together, Hera and its CubeSats will more precisely determine the mass of Dimorphos, which, when combined with information about the orbital change of the system, will be crucial in planning missions to deflect threatening asteroids.

Sources indicate that hera's observations were revealed on Wednesday (Nov. 25) at the dinosaur hall of the Museum für Naturkunde Berlin, Germany. That location isn't a coincidence: It is a stark reminder of why this planetary defense mission is so crucial. Especially if humanity doesn't want to go the way of the dinosaurs, whose rule on Earth ended when an asteroid fell from the sky."Sixty-six million years ago, an asteroid impact changed the course of life on Earth. Today, for the first time in history, humanity is validating how to prevent such an event from happening again," Hera mission manager Ian Carnelli explained. "NASA's DART mission demonstrated that we can change an asteroid's orbit. Hera is now revealing what happened to the asteroid itself. "By combining these two missions, humanity is taking a decisive step towards making asteroid deflection a reliable tool for protecting our planet.".

He also writes about science communication for Elsevier and the European Journal of Physics. Rob holds a bachelor of science degree in physics and astronomy from the U.K.’s Open University. Marco Rose replaced Andoni Iraola - who ended up at Liverpool - in the summer.

Bournemouth are dreaming of winning the Europa League after staging a 10-man fightback to join a select band of teams to win their first five European games.

The Cherries trailed 1-0 to Iago Aspas' goal at Celta Vigo, and then went down to 10 men midway through the first half when Bafode Diakite was sent off.

But second-half goals from Alvaro Rodriguez and Rayan gave the Cherries a 10th consecutive win in all competitions, extending their club record run.

Bournemouth are only the third side to win each of their first five European matches (excluding qualifiers and including the Inter-Cities Fairs Cup), after Nuremberg in 1961-62 and Ararat in 1972-73.

They top this season's table as the only club to win five out of five - and are closing in on a top-eight spot, which would mean they skip a play-off round and go straight into the last 16.

Some fans have told the BBC they have already booked hotels in Frankfurt for the final on 26 May.

As supporters sang about reaching that game, midfielder Alex Scott was asked for his thoughts on TNT Sports.

Recent findings suggest that "Of course that's our dream. When you grow up wanting to be a footballer you dream of winning trophies," Scott said.

"Where this club has come from to where it is now, full credit to everyone who has built it.

In a recent development, "For players, it's a dream to be on the pitch playing for this club. We have still got wins to get to qualify into the top eight, and from there all focus is on pushing forward and hopefully we can go on and win it.".

The Cherries are in unprecedented times, with their biggest trophy to date being when they won the second-tier Championship in 2014-15.

In terms of cups, they won the 1983â84 Associate Members' Cup - which later became the EFL Trophy.

Head coach Marco Rose, who replaced Andoni Iraola in the summer, stated: "It's always allowed to dream.

"If you get a competition like this you want to achieve the best possible thing. We know it's far away to go. Many games. Now it's about getting into the top eight to avoid more games and then we can see step by step.".

As well as just winning their games, Bournemouth are firing in the goals. They have netted at least twice in each match during this 10-game winning run.

And they are the first side to score at least twice in each of their first five matches in Europe since Queens Park Rangers in 1976.

The win on Thursday was made even more impressive by the fact they contested 75% of the game with 10 men.

It came days after Manchester United seemed to implode after an early red card against Liverpool, losing 4-0.

Industry observers note that former England manager Glenn Hoddle said on TNT: "They have deserved this result. They've played beautifully with 10 men - probably as good as I've seen a team play defensively and with the ball.

In a recent development, "I've not seen a team go down to 10 men for so long and dictate a game and deserve to win the game. They were absolutely brilliant.".

Cherries boss Rose told BBC Radio Solent: "What a team, what a spirit, what an energy.

"I said to Ty [Tyler Adams] sometimes it's not about tactics and formations and stuff like this. [David] Brooks did a great job when we got one player less - he played right defender like he played it for 10 years. We changed in the right moment. Everyone did his job on a really high level.

"We were just relentless and we never stopped to believe in this win and that's why significant, big, big congratulations to the team.

"You feel if you're one player down that it's a difficult night, but to handle a difficult night like this, it just highlights the character of the team and of the whole group.".

The coach's belief in what they are doing filters through to the players.

Amine Adli, who set up the equaliser, told the BBC: "At half-time, everyone still believed we can turn the game in our way and this is what happened.

"Everyone was like 'guys we can make it, we have to believe. If we score the game can change.'".

Earlier this month, the attacking midfielder noted he saw a lot of similarities to the Bayer Leverkusen team he was part of in 2023-24.

That is not a bad comparison, considering they went unbeaten to win the domestic double, as well as reaching the Europa League final.

So who can blame the Cherries for dreaming?

Police in several locations across Germany reported large numbers of bomb threats targeting schools.

They mentioned that while they were investigating the claims, they did not initially have reason to treat them as credible threats.

More than 400 schools in the southwestern state of Baden Württemberg received threats, and more than 250 in Saxony-Anhalt received the emails, with several other regions also targeted on Monday morning.

Police in Erfurt in Thuringia were among the first to issue a statement on the threats, saying they were responding to threats at "multiple schools" after morning warnings, including in Jena, Erfurt, Mühlhausen, Zella-Mehlis, Nordhausen, Gotha, Rudolstadt and Greiz.

"The same word-for-word threats were received this morning at the various eductional institutes," police wrote in a press release. "Based on preliminary findings other federal states are also affected by the threatening messages.".

Sources indicate that police mentioned they had no information yet on the potential author or sender of the emails. They were investigating breach of the peace-based crimes via the threat of criminal activity.

"At present the police is not working on the assumption of the bomb threats being serious and recommends that schools do not implement evacuation measures and continue their normal operations," they mentioned.

Police in Freiburg in the southwest and authorities to the north in Hanover also noted they were responding to emailed bomb threats directed against schools.

Similar reports are emerging to the north of Germany in Denmark.

As in Germany, Danish police remarked they did not believe the threats were credible, "but they understandably create insecurity locally at the schools.".

This follows other recent cases of coordinated bomb threats against multiple schools that turned out to be hoaxes in Italy earlier in the month.

It also comes amid various apparent bids to create disruption within Europe in recent weeks, such as multiple bomb threats targeting commercial airlines, or hacking into supermarket refrigeration systems to spoil produce en masse.

According to recent reports, “It’s OK,” Kotb remarked on the November 25 episode of Late Night With Seth Meyers. “We waited 100 years for this parade, we’re gonna wait two more days. We’re gonna have it on Saturday. It’s gonna be a beautiful, sunsplash day.”.

“Thank you to the thousands of volunteers, performers and partners who create the magic millions enjoy each year,” a spokesperson told MSNOW in a statement. “We look forward to celebrating together on Saturday.”.
