CERN scientists finally find evidence of a particle decay so rare it took 40 years to detect

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1469 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that after more than four decades of searching, physicists at CERN have finally found evidence of an extraordinarily rare particle decay that occurs only about once in every 10 billion beauty particles.
  • According to recent reports, the evidence comes from the upgraded LHCb experiment at CERN's Large Hadron Collider (LHC).
  • The elusive process, called 'Bd to mu mu', has a statistical significance of 3.2 sigma.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that after more than four decades of searching, physicists at CERN have finally found evidence of an extraordinarily rare particle decay that occurs only about once in every 10 billion beauty particles. The long-awaited result could help scientists investigate a largely unexplored realm of physics where unknown particles and forces of nature may exist.

According to recent reports, the evidence comes from the upgraded LHCb experiment at CERN's Large Hadron Collider (LHC). Researchers at the University of Manchester played key roles in the international effort, contributing to the advanced technology that made the measurement possible.

The elusive process, called 'Bd to mu mu', has a statistical significance of 3.2 sigma. That is strong enough to qualify as evidence, but physicists will need additional data before they can officially declare a discovery. Even so, the finding marks a major milestone in a search that has lasted more than 40 years.

In a recent development, it also creates new opportunities to test the Standard Model, the leading scientific framework describing fundamental particles and how they interact. By examining this exceptionally rare decay in greater detail, researchers hope to uncover subtle clues that could eventually point toward physics beyond our current understanding.

Why Rare Particle Decays Could Reveal New Physics.

The LHCb experiment specializes in studying particles that contain beauty quarks. These are heavier relatives of the up and down quarks that make up much of the ordinary matter around us.

It has been revealed that when particles collide inside the Large Hadron Collider, enormous numbers of beauty quarks are produced. However, they survive for only about one and a half trillionths of a second before decaying into other particles.

Scientists study these transformations because they may reveal the influence of particles that cannot be directly observed at the collider. By measuring exactly how frequently different decays occur, physicists can search for unexpected effects that might indicate previously unknown physics.

It has been revealed that particularly rare decays offer an important advantage. Because they happen so infrequently, their rates can be especially sensitive to contributions from undiscovered particles. Even small differences between predicted and observed decay rates could provide valuable evidence of upcoming forces or particles.

A One in 10 Billion Particle Decay.

The newly observed signal involves a process known as 'Bd to mu mu'. During this decay, a particle containing a beauty quark transforms into two muons, which are heavier relatives of electrons.

Sources indicate that according to theoretical predictions, this transformation should occur only about once in every 10 billion beauty particles. Despite decades of investigation, no individual experiment had previously produced convincing evidence that it occurs.

The upgraded LHCb experiment has now achieved a statistical significance of 3.2 sigma. Although this meets the standard for reporting evidence, particle physicists generally require a significance of five sigma before announcing a confirmed discovery.

Sources indicate that professor Chris Parkes, Head of the Department of Physics and Astronomy at the University of Manchester, led the international LHCb collaboration during construction of its major upgrade. He also oversaw the collaboration's approval of the fresh findings.

He explained: "The upgraded LHCb was a major undertaking -- a fifteen-year design and construction project from a 1900 international member collaboration.

"The UK made the largest national contribution to the project, pioneering latest technologies that have made today's result possible, where we probe nature at a new scale. But this is also just the start; we are planning the construction of an experiment that will exploit the capabilities of the next-generation High Luminosity LHC, probing physics at an even smaller scale.".

Parkes, who became a Fellow of the Royal Society earlier this year in recognition of his contributions to LHCb, offered a memorable comparison to illustrate just how improbable the decay is.

"This decay is remarkably unlikely; the chance of it happening is roughly like going on a romantic date and, on your very first try, finding the one perfect match for you among everyone on Earth.".

Advanced LHC Detectors Make the Breakthrough Possible.

Detecting such an uncommon event requires instruments capable of following the movements of particles with extraordinary accuracy.

One of the most important components of the upgraded LHCb experiment is a silicon pixel detector developed with major contributions from researchers in the United Kingdom. Called the Vertex Locator, it measures the paths of particles generated during collisions inside the collider.

Positioned just five millimeters from the LHC beams, the detector allows researchers to determine precisely where particles originate and where they subsequently decay.

Industry observers note that dr. Stefano De Capua, who directed detector construction at the University of Manchester, described the extensive collaboration behind the technology.

Sources indicate that "We worked with nearly 90 UK companies to construct this detector and trained the next generation of scientists and engineers on the novel technologies we are using. It is these detectors that we use to locate where the beauty meson was produced and pinpoint where it decayed into two muons.".

The wider LHCb upgrade also allows the experiment to gather information at up to five times its previous rate. This greater capacity, together with improvements in tracking technology, is helping physicists identify events that were previously too difficult to measure reliably.

Exploring the Mysterious Zeptoverse.

Beyond confirming an exceptionally rare particle process, the result could help scientists investigate what they call the 'Zeptoverse'.

Industry observers note that this name refers to an almost unimaginably small scale, measured in zeptometers. A single zeptometer is just a billionth of a trillionth of a meter. Physicists suspect that effects from currently unknown particles and forces could become apparent when nature is examined at these extreme scales.

It has been revealed that for now, the upcoming measurement agrees with the Standard Model. Researchers have not found evidence that the established theory is wrong, but increasingly precise measurements could reveal deviations that current experiments cannot yet detect.

Such differences would be especially significant because they could indicate where the Standard Model stops providing a complete explanation of the physical world.

Professor Conor Fitzpatrick of the University of Manchester, who serves as Deputy Physics Coordinator of the international LHCb collaboration, emphasized the importance of finally obtaining the long-sought signal.

"There has been a more than forty year long search by physicists worldwide to observe this decay. It is a golden channel to observe the effects of newly introduced physics from beyond our current knowledge.

Recent findings suggest that "The results from this experiment are expanding our understanding of nature at its most fundamental level. We are excited to have finally seen this elusive signal and looking forward to the future discoveries that will come from our data.".

What Comes Next for CERN's Particle Research?

Sources indicate that the upgraded LHCb experiment is expected to continue gathering a substantially larger collection of measurements into the early 2030s. With more data, physicists should be able to determine the frequency of this rare decay with much greater precision.

Industry observers note that researchers are also planning another major upgrade that could increase data collection rates by an additional factor of ten. This would improve their ability to investigate extremely rare particle processes and search for the effects of unknown particles at even smaller distance scales.

Professor Brian Cox, a particle physicist at the University of Manchester who did not participate in the experiment, highlighted how improvements in scientific instruments can lead to key advances in understanding nature.

Recent findings suggest that "This is an vital result and a beautiful example of how science advances. We upgrade our instruments, and we see nature in greater detail. Occasionally we see something we don't understand, and then progress is made. We cannot know whether this progress will be incremental or genuinely world-changing -- that's science! LHCb is a major scientific success.".

Recent findings suggest that the experiment receives funding from the Science and Technology Facilities Council, which operates within UK Research and Innovation. The UK LHCb collaboration brings together scientists from ten universities across the United Kingdom and the STFC Rutherford Appleton Laboratory.

Recent findings suggest that although the newly detected decay has not yet revealed any unknown particles or forces, it gives physicists a powerful new way to search for them. After more than 40 years of effort, an extraordinarily elusive process is finally becoming accessible to detailed study, potentially bringing researchers closer to understanding some of the universe's deepest mysteries.

US tech organization Nvidia stated on Monday that it had reinstated Jensen Huang as its CEO "effective immediately.".

This follows just a matter of days after his resignation after admitting to extramarital affairs, reportedly including a dalliance with a woman who was a Chinese intelligence asset.

The board unanimously decided that his return was in the "best interests of the manufacturer," Nvidia noted, adding that it was satisfied that Huang had demonstrated his "candor and ability to lead.".

Meanwhile, the 63-year-old mentioned in a statement that he was "honored" to return to the company and that he would take on the renewed responsibility "with the greatest humility and renewed commitment.".

He thanked interim CEO Colette Kress, who is set to return to her role as chief financial officer.

"I am also deeply thankful to our employees, shareholders, leaders across the industry and partners around the world for their extraordinary support," Huang said. "Above all, I am grateful for the love and support of my family. I can't wait to get back to work.".

US President Donald Trump rapidly commented on the development online, saying it was the "correct and proper decision" and referring to Huang by his first name as a "Great Patriot and National Treasure.".

"The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen's return to Nvidia poses any risk to National Security," Trump wrote, also saying that the US had no evidence of him engaging in unlawful conduct.

Sources indicate that huang liked to flaunt his personal relationship with Trump. He was reportedly influential in convincing the US president to allow the export of higher-quality Nvidia chips to China that are useful in AI development than other US officials and entrepreneurs endorsed.

The decision was revealed as trading started for the new week in New York.

The stock price of what investors deem the world's most valuable company has nosedived amid the scandal, with Nvidia's stock price falling from almost $220 (roughly €200) per share in late October to around $125 per share at the end of last week.

The announcement prompted a rapid early-morning rally on Wall Street, including Nvidia stocks rising back into a region between $160 and $170.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

Hims & Hers releases latest peptide treatments — while admitting there's more to learn about efficacy

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1567 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that hims & Hers Health on Wednesday said it will offer five formulations of peptides and longevity treatments compounded in the U.S.
  • Even as it announced the new products, Hims & Hers acknowledged it has more to learn about how best to use the peptides and how effective they are — underscoring the uncertainty surrounding the growing space.
  • In a recent development, the upcoming offerings come after the federal government eased restrictions on compounding certain unapproved peptides, which are short chains of amino ​acids.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that hims & Hers Health on Wednesday said it will offer five formulations of peptides and longevity treatments compounded in the U.S. as part of the initial rollout of its Peptides+ platform, all of which are not approved by regulators.

Even as it announced the new products, Hims & Hers acknowledged it has more to learn about how best to use the peptides and how effective they are — underscoring the uncertainty surrounding the growing space.

In a recent development, the upcoming offerings come after the federal government eased restrictions on compounding certain unapproved peptides, which are short chains of amino ​acids. Those products have exploded in popularity among fitness and longevity enthusiasts who attest that they help with muscle growth, rapid injury recovery and anti-aging, even though most lack evidence from robust human trials.

Hims in late October rolled out an early access list for the upcoming peptide offerings, and more than 10,000 people signed up within 15 days, a organization spokesperson said in a statement.

Sources indicate that none of the tech giant's specific compounded products are approved by the Food and Drug Administration. But Hims noted they are authorized by law and formulated by pharmacies "that adhere to rigorous quality standards and are licensed and inspected by state boards of pharmacy.".

The products include compounded formulations of sermorelin, a peptide that stimulates growth-hormone release and is marketed for recovery, body composition and anti-aging; glutathione, a peptide promoted ‌for anti-aging and athletic recovery; and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide, or NAD+, a coenzyme that plays a role in cellular metabolism.

The company will also offer compounded versions of vitamin B-12, a vitamin needed to make red blood cells, build DNA, and maintain healthy nerve function, and L-carnitine, an amino acid derivative that helps the body turn fat into energy. The FDA has approved certain prescription forms of both peptides for established medical uses, primarily for diagnosed deficiencies in those compounds.

Recent findings suggest that hims stated it intends to add more peptides and therapies made in the U.S. over time. That includes BPC-157, an unapproved peptide derived from a protein found in human gastric juice that is marketed for healing processes. The company also aims to introduce another unapproved peptide called TB-500, which is derived from a naturally occurring protein in the body and is marketed for broader, systemic soft-tissue recovery and flexibility. Most of the research on both has been conducted in animals, not humans.

To receive the products, members on the Hims platform will start with an assessment of health history and goals with a licensed provider trained in peptide therapies, who can tailor a personalized plan to their needs, if appropriate.

The company mentioned it intends to use its communication platform to check in with patients and ensure they are seeing desired results.

"If they're not, we need to do something about it," Dr. Anant Vinjamoori, Hims chief medical officer, told CNBC. "We need to, you know, adjust the dose when that's appropriate, or in some cases consider other compounds that's maybe a better fit. And of course, there will also be cases when we need to refer people to other care options.".

However, Vinjamoori said there's still uncertainty over how to best use the peptides.

Industry observers note that "We don't have all of this data that we're used to having with compounds like this," he noted. "We have the opportunity to get it right, and I think we see that as our responsibility with a company of our size, our skill, and resources to really lead.".

Vinjamoori added that people who have serious illnesses, such as cardiovascular disease, liver disease and kidney disease, will not be candidates for the compounds for now.

Meanwhile, Andrew Huberman, a well known neuroscientist, podcaster and Stanford University School of Medicine professor who recently joined Hims' board of directors, in a statement called compounds "real medical treatments, not just a wellness trend." He said Hims provides safe access through "trusted sourcing and physician oversight.".

But health experts raised concerns about the broader mainstream marketing of peptides in the U.S. and accessing them on telehealth platforms.

"With peptides, I think you have to view them the same way you would view any drug that hasn't been rigorously tested," said Joshua Kritzer, a chemistry professor at Tufts University. "Without actual testing, all you have is anecdotal information, and that's just not enough information to put a substance in your body.".

Kritzer remarked the lack of large clinical trials means researchers can't rule out potentially serious, rare complications from peptides — the kinds of risks that have led regulators to reject or pull otherwise effective drugs from the market after they underwent comprehensive testing in humans.

Sources indicate that without that testing, it's also unclear how telehealth firms, physicians and pharmacies can make decisions about what doses patients should take, stated Paul Knoepfler, a cell biology and human anatomy professor at UC Davis Health. While some people rely on anecdotal data from real peptide users, "the dosing for these products really has not been established," he added.

Knoepfler stated one risk is that injecting too much of a synthetic peptide into patients could trigger "weird immune responses that are really bad for one's health" because the body might recognize it as foreign.

"With the peptides, it's very loosey-goosey," Knoepfler told CNBC. "How does one even know what would be the effective amount for whatever you're hoping it will do, and what amount would have more risks?".

According to recent reports, but he said the more contact patients can have with physicians around taking a compounded peptide, the better. Providers, including those tied to telehealth firms, should make sure patients are well-informed about the possible risks and unknowns of a given product and consider their preexisting conditions, cancer history and other medications, Knoepfler said.

That appears to be consistent with the approach Hims & Hers is taking. The tech giant notes patients who use the peptide and longevity products can also use its Care+ offering, which pairs treatment with ongoing support. That includes twice-a-year lab testing to track their progress and the ability to message providers trained in peptide therapy around the clock with any questions.

Still, Kritzer argued that having a doctor who only knows a patient from online, essentially mail-order platforms or websites "is not enough supervision to put you on a prescription medication," especially an unapproved one.

Hims' ability to legally sell some of these peptides stems from a major shift in federal oversight by the Health and Human Services Department. It issued a policy in October that claims the Food and Drug Administration will not take enforcement action against licensed pharmacies, federal facilities or physicians that compound and dispense six unapproved peptides while formal rules are reviewed.

According to recent reports, in practice, that means these pharmacies and other firms can now offer them, even though the peptides aren't yet on the FDA's official list of ingredients compounding pharmacies are allowed to make. It does not translate to formal approval of the specific peptides.

The policy followed a 2023 decision by the Biden administration where the FDA restricted compounding pharmacies from producing popular peptide formulations due to safety, impurity and immune-reaction concerns.

Industry observers note that HHS Secretary ​Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has supported broader access to peptides, calling himself a "massive fan" of the treatments and arguing that restrictions were driving Americans to potentially unsafe products from overseas. Kennedy has previously described using BPC-157 to treat a muscle injury.

The announcement also comes after Hims in February 2025 acquired a California-based peptide manufacturing facility equipped with advanced peptide synthesizers.

The evidence for peptide efficacy varies by compound.

A 2026 systematic review screening 113 studies, including both small trials on humans along with rodent research, found zero eligible clinical outcome trials proving that administering IV or intramuscular NAD+ improves anti-aging, energy, or wellness endpoints in humans.

There is some evidence for specific uses of certain peptides, such as potential weight loss. A review of 37 L-carnitine trials found participants lost about 2.7 pounds on average, though that analysis does not demonstrate that a compounded injection works the same way.

Meanwhile, vitamin B-12 injections are most commonly used to help people with a diagnosed deficiency rather than preventative care. U.S. survey data shows only 3.6% of adults are B-12 deficient.

Sources indicate that glutathione's evidence is thin, too. IV injections of it are widely marketed for skin whitening, yet not FDA-approved for this purpose.

A small study published in the Journal of Pakistan Association of Dermatologists evaluating IV glutathione revealed that the treatment is "not very effective" for skin-lightening, and that it loses efficacy with time.

The FDA also noted in August that it received reports of at least 30 patients who experienced adverse events after they received compounded IV glutathione alone or in combination with other ingredients from different compounding pharmacies.

All of the glutathione tied to the reports were from the same wholesale distributor and was labeled as dietary supplement grade, which is not an appropriate ingredient to make injectable drugs. Two of the Texas pharmacies conducted recalls related to elevated endotoxin levels in their glutathione injectable drugs.

These studies and reports don't speak to how Hims' exact combination will perform, but they do highlight the current limits on data studying the treatments and the questions surrounding them.

#208169. A 50-year-old theory about evolution may have been wrong all along

A 50-year-old theory about evolution may have been wrong all along

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1259 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For more than 50 years, scientists have debated a provocative idea about evolution: Could organisms protect their most crucial genes by making them less likely to mutate?
  • In a study published in PLOS Biology, Dr.
  • Industry observers note that the findings challenge the claim that natural selection can reduce mutation rates in genes essential for survival.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For more than 50 years, scientists have debated a provocative idea about evolution: Could organisms protect their most crucial genes by making them less likely to mutate? First proposed in 1972, the hypothesis challenges the traditional understanding of how genetic changes arise. Now, upcoming research from the University of Bath suggests that the evidence supporting this idea has been misleading.

In a study published in PLOS Biology, Dr. Sofia Radrizzani and Professor Laurence D Hurst of the University of Bath's Centre for Evolution examined the largest collection of spontaneous genetic mutations assembled to date. Their analysis focused on two microorganisms: the bacterium Escherichia coli (E. coli) and the single-celled fungus baker's yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae).

Industry observers note that the findings challenge the claim that natural selection can reduce mutation rates in genes essential for survival. Although this theory has repeatedly attracted scientific attention since its introduction, including a renewed debate in 2023, the researchers say their results undermine its central premise.

"The claim that mutation is slower for important genes is a triumph of hype over substance," noted Dr. Radrizzani, who co-wrote the fresh paper as part of her PhD. "It's a really old suggestion and is reinvented in various forms routinely.".

How Mutations and Natural Selection Drive Evolution.

The conventional explanation of evolution involves two main processes. Genetic mutations first introduce variation among organisms. Natural selection then influences which of those variations become more common, favoring traits that improve survival and reproduction. This process can be compared to a sieve that separates different kinds of material, allowing some genetic changes to persist while others disappear.

A familiar example comes from Darwin's finches, which Charles Darwin first encountered on the Galápagos Islands in 1835. These birds have different beak shapes that help them feed on different foods. Random mutations contribute to variations in beak size and shape, and when certain food sources become more plentiful, birds with better-suited beaks are more likely to survive and reproduce. Over many generations, these advantageous traits can spread through the population.

It has been revealed that however, an alternative hypothesis suggests that mutations may not occur as randomly as the conventional model assumes. According to this idea, organisms have evolved ways to reduce mutations in their most critical genes (such as those involved in replicating DNA or maintaining basic cellular machinery). Meanwhile, genes in which changes might provide useful adaptations (such as those in which mutations give bacteria resistance to antibiotics, or change beak dimensions) could experience higher mutation rates.

At first glance, protecting essential genes seems like an obvious evolutionary advantage. Mutations affecting these genes can disrupt vital biological processes, cause genetic diseases, or even kill an organism. If such changes are so dangerous, why wouldn't natural selection favor mechanisms that prevent them?

In a recent development, the problem, researchers explain, is that mutations in individual genes are already relatively rare. Reducing those rates even further would provide only a tiny additional benefit, making it difficult for natural selection to favor such a protective system.

The Mystery of Disappearing Genetic Mutations.

In a recent development, another problem lies in how scientists have measured mutations in earlier research. Notable genes may appear to mutate less frequently not because they are better protected, but because harmful mutations in those genes are quickly eliminated from populations.

It has been revealed that professor Hurst noted: "We'd expect natural selection to rapidly remove mutations when they occur in more crucial genes, because these mutations are more likely to be harmful to the organism. This can create the illusion that important genes have fewer mutations when, in reality, some mutations have simply disappeared before we have a chance to analyze them - what you can think of as 'ghost mutations'.".

In a recent development, this distinction is crucial. When scientists examine the genetic changes remaining in a population, they may miss mutations that occurred but were subsequently removed by natural selection. As a result, the apparent stability of essential genes could reflect the disappearance of damaging mutations rather than a lower likelihood of those mutations occurring in the first place.

A Major Test of the 50-Year-Old Evolutionary Theory.

To investigate the question more directly, the University of Bath team analyzed data from experiments designed to record mutations while minimizing the influence of natural selection. These experiments, known as mutation accumulation studies, allowed researchers to examine genetic changes in E. coli and baker's yeast without the usual strong filtering effects of selection.

Sources indicate that the scientists also performed three independent tests to determine whether natural selection might still have significantly distorted the data. None revealed evidence of substantial bias.

Industry observers note that dr. Radrizzani noted: "This looks like the largest and cleanest sample of mutations assembled to date.".

With this extensive dataset, the researchers investigated whether genes that are more vital for survival actually experience fewer mutations.

In a recent development, they assessed gene importance using experiments in which individual genes were removed from organisms. Some genes are indispensable, meaning that cells die without them. Others can be deleted with little or no noticeable effect.

If the protective mutation hypothesis were correct, the most essential genes should have shown consistently lower mutation rates. Instead, the researchers found no such relationship in either microorganism.

Industry observers note that professor Hurst said: "Analyze the data any which way and we found nothing. In neither species did these key genes have a lower mutation rate.".

What Really Determines How Often Genes Mutate?

The team also examined whether other measures of gene importance could explain differences in mutation rates. These included the amount of protein produced by each gene and how strongly natural selection had shaped genes over thousands of years.

Once again, the results failed to support the idea that more vital genes receive special protection.

Industry observers note that dr. Radrizzani noted: "We found that genes producing more abundant proteins don't have lower mutation rates. Nor does the way genes evolve over thousands of years predict how frequently they mutate.".

According to recent reports, that does not mean every gene has exactly the same chance of mutating. The researchers identified features of genome structure and DNA replication that influence mutation frequency. For example, genes copied later during DNA replication tend to accumulate mutations more frequently than those copied earlier.

These findings indicate that mutation rates can vary across the genome, but the differences do not appear to reflect a system that specifically shields essential genes from genetic changes.

In a recent development, professor Hurst stated: "While we see known causes of variation in mutation rates, we found no evidence for the effects that have been proposed as a challenge to the conventional model. None predicted which genes would have high or low mutation rates, and there are certainly no grounds for a shift in paradigm.".

Sources indicate that the research therefore provides new support for the conventional distinction between mutation and natural selection. Although mutations do not occur at identical rates everywhere in the genome, the evidence from bacteria and yeast offers no indication that evolution systematically protects its most important genes by reducing how often they mutate.

It has been revealed that "This action opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America's leadership and growth," FCC Chairman Brendan Carr mentioned today (Nov. 25) in a statement announcing the approval.

According to recent reports, AI has become central to SpaceX's business aims and identity over the past year or so. For example, the company has said that it's eyeing a "total addressable market" of $28.5 trillion over the long haul — and nearly $23 trillion of that is in "enterprise AI applications.".

It has been revealed that starmind is key to those lofty ambitions. SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk believes that the future of AI compute is in space, where energy (from the sun) is unlimited and there are no land-owning neighbors to lodge NIMBY complaints.

Industry observers note that spaceX aims to launch the first of its Starmind satellites in the third quarter of 2027. The spacecraft will fly on the company's fully reusable Starship megarocket, which has deployed 26 of SpaceX's next-gen Starlink satellites on its most recent two test flights.

Those 52 spacecraft are the vanguard of another enormous constellation: Musk has stated that the next-gen Starlink network will eventually consists of about 100,000 satellites.

The planned numbers for Starlink and Starmind are truly mind-boggling. To put them into perspective: Since the dawn of the space age in 1957, humanity has introduced a total of just 28,000 satellites, give or take a few hundred. And the biggest constellation ever operated to date, the current iteration of Starlink, consists of about 11,000 spacecraft.

Industry observers note that these coming buildouts will require an enormous number of launches. Starship can carry a maximum of 60 V3 Starlink satellites per launch, for instance, so it will take about 1,700 liftoffs just to assemble that network (and more to maintain it, as the operational life of each satellite is expected to be about five years).

It has been revealed that putting so many satellites into orbit also raises the risks of collisions. SpaceX has proven to be extremely proficient in this regard with its current Starlink satellites, which can detect and avoid potential collisions autonomously. But more evasive maneuvers will be required as space gets more and more crowded.

Sources indicate that spaceX isn't the only company that aims to operate data centers in space; Cowboy Space, Starcloud, Blue Origin and Google, among other companies, have voiced similar ambitions. Starcloud and Google, in fact, have already debuted AI pathfinder satellites.

"Compute campuses or data centers are essential to sustaining America's leadership in SI," Carr stated in the same statement. ("SI" stands for super intelligence, the Trump administration's preferred term for AI.).

According to recent reports, "By moving compute capacity beyond Earth, SpaceX and the many competitors working on their own orbital data centers are meeting the moment," Carr added. "This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home.".

Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. To find out what his latest project is, you can follow Michael on Twitter.

Industry News: Even scientists can't agree on what science actually is

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (786 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that scientists dedicate their careers to uncovering how the world works, yet they have surprisingly different opinions about what science actually means.
  • The study, published in Royal Society Open Science, examined 18 different descriptions of science and found that researchers rarely embraced any of them without reservations.
  • "What was surprising to me was that there was quite a bit of disagreement between scientists, including scientists who are in the same subfield," states Marina Dubova, who led the research while working as a postdoctoral researcher at the Santa Fe Institute.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that scientists dedicate their careers to uncovering how the world works, yet they have surprisingly different opinions about what science actually means. Latest research reveals that scientists disagree about the nature and purpose of science even more than the general public does.

The study, published in Royal Society Open Science, examined 18 different descriptions of science and found that researchers rarely embraced any of them without reservations. Even when scientists generally supported a particular definition, many questioned some aspect of it.

"What was surprising to me was that there was quite a bit of disagreement between scientists, including scientists who are in the same subfield," states Marina Dubova, who led the research while working as a postdoctoral researcher at the Santa Fe Institute.

Members of the public, by comparison, expressed more consistent views. They were more likely to regard science as a dependable way to discover objective truths about the world, placing less importance on the uncertainty and creativity involved in scientific research.

These contrasting perspectives may have notable consequences. They could affect the questions scientists choose to investigate and influence how people evaluate scientific findings. They may also help explain why the public sometimes becomes frustrated when researchers cannot offer clear answers or change their conclusions in response to new evidence.

What Scientists and the Public Believe About Science.

It has been revealed that dubova, now an assistant professor of psychology at the University of California, Berkeley, worked with Princeton University researcher Qiawen E. Liu to investigate how people understand science.

The researchers surveyed 91 scientists and 99 members of the public. Participants were asked to assess 18 descriptions of science drawn from historical perspectives, including comparisons of scientific research to detective work, a pursuit of truth, and a mirror that reflects reality.

Both groups generally agreed that curiosity, exploration, and the desire to solve mysteries are central to science. Beyond those shared ideas, however, the scientists expressed strikingly different perspectives.

Sources indicate that some researchers viewed science primarily as a means of discovering objective truths. Others placed greater importance on imagination, personal judgment, and the creative decisions involved in research. Scientists also differed over whether scientific progress depends mainly on following established procedures or adapting and improvising as new challenges arise.

According to recent reports, dubova believes these disagreements may reflect the individual experiences that shape how researchers approach their work. Just as chefs can have very different philosophies about preparing food, scientists can develop distinct ideas about the best ways to investigate the world.

Why the Public Sees Science Differently.

Industry observers note that another intriguing finding involved differences among scientific disciplines. The general public's understanding of science more closely resembled the views expressed by physicists and biologists than those of psychologists and other social scientists.

One possible reason is that physics and biology receive greater attention in science education, potentially shaping how people imagine scientific research. Dubova emphasizes, however, that this explanation remains tentative and will require additional investigation.

The differences between scientists and the public could also help explain misunderstandings about scientific uncertainty. People who expect science to produce firm, objective answers may have difficulty understanding why findings sometimes conflict or why scientific conclusions must be updated when upcoming evidence becomes available.

What the Findings Could Mean for AI and Scientific Discovery.

The research also points to a potential challenge as artificial intelligence becomes increasingly involved in scientific discovery.

Sources indicate that with researchers developing AI systems that can carry out scientific investigations, Dubova is concerned that automation could favor a limited conception of how science should work. If those systems are built around one particular approach to research, other valuable methods of discovery could receive less attention.

It has been revealed that the study received support from the Santa Fe Institute's Lou Schuyler Seed Grant Fund, which was created in 2022 to encourage exploratory projects by early career scientists. Dubova used the funding to pay participants for taking part in the research.

For Dubova, the findings represent an initial effort to understand how scientists' underlying beliefs about their profession might influence the research they conduct and the discoveries they make.

In a recent development, "Don't take the common understanding of science for granted," she claims. "Always ask. Always be curious about what someone has in mind.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Julianne Hough is spinning away from the negativity.

After the Dancing With the Stars cohost made waves for her fashion choices during season 35, she shed insight into her looks while responding to those who gave a low score on her style.

Recent findings suggest that “I really feel like I’m at this next inflection of my career,” Hough told Glamour in an interview published Nov. 24 alongside her stylist Brad Goreski. “When you get into your late 30s, you just don’t give a f--k anymore. You’re like, ‘Who am I? What do I want to wear? What makes me feel incredible?’ It has more intention rather than trying to fit into what’s hot.”.

“I feel like I’m in my leading lady era,” she continued. “I mean that in the actual projects that I’m doing, but also me as a person.”.

To cohost this season of DWTS alongside Alfonso Ribeiro, the professional dancer decided to take a step out of her comfort zone.

“I’ve gone a little bit more vixen-y this year than I have girl next door because we’re trying to find that character,” she shared. “It’s been very strategic.”.

Recent findings suggest that as she twirled with a new vibe, Hough took some fashion risks, including a sultry Valentino ensemble—which featured a skin-colored leotard under a see-through skirt—during the Nov. 17 episode that really had fans talking, with one social media user calling for Hough’s stylist to be “fired” in a viral Instagram video.

But as for Goreski, he doesn’t believe the online chatter about Hough’s looks is completely pointe-less anyway, emphasizing that “any conversation, good or bad, around fashion is great.”.

Sources indicate that “I think Jules ultimately brings the looks to life,” he added, praising his client. “I’m glad that there’s another part of the show that people talk about. Not every person’s going to love every look. I know that from being a stylist for 15 years. And that’s okay.”.

And ultimately, Hough concluded that taking those fashion risks is worth it, despite what people may say.

Sources indicate that “Apathy is the enemy,” she said, sharing the phrase became her motto for the season. “The reason things exist and have charge and stay visible [is] people either love it or hate it. They still want to talk about it.”.

As Hough and DWTS wrap up another season, read on for a deep dive into the TV series….

How Much Do the Celebrities Get Paid to Be on Dancing With the Stars?

It has been revealed that citing multiple sources, Variety reported in 2019 that Dancing With the Stars contestants make $125,000 for the rehearsal period and first two weeks of the show. If they progress beyond that point, the outlet continued, they earn more money each week. At the time, sources told the publication stars could earn a maximum of $295,000.

However, Bobby Bones remarked he made more than this when he won season 27 with Sharna Burgess in 2018.

"That show pays OK," the radio personality noted on a Sept. 2025 episode of Jason Tartick's podcast Trading Secrets. "Like, first episode, no money. Second episode, $10,000. I think it's like, $10,000, $10,000, $20,000, $20,000. It ends up being $50,000 an episode if you last.".

Also receiving a base salary of around $110,000, Bones continued, "I ended up making close to $400,000 from that show.".

ABC has not publicly confirmed any of these figures.

What Do the Pros Get Paid on Dancing With the Stars?

In a recent development, similarly, little has been shared publicly about how much the pros get paid. But as with the contestants, it seems like the longer they're on the show, the more money they can make.

But even if a pro is eliminated in the first round, they're not leaving the ballroom empty-handed.

Industry observers note that "You're guaranteed until a certain amount of weeks," Jenna Johnson mentioned on a June 2025 episode of Kelly Stafford and Hank Winchester's podcast The Morning After. "I think there's different contracts though. I can't speak for everybody.".

Do Pros Get Paid More If They Win Dancing With the Stars?

While Johnson—who won season 26 with Olympic figure skater Adam Rippon, as well as season 33 with The Bachelor's Joey Graziadei—says the pros don't get a larger paycheck if they take home what is now called the Len Goodman Mirrorball Trophy, she noted there's still an incentive to make it to the finale (besides bragging rights, of course).

"If you make it all the way to the end, you're getting paid the whole season, which is amazing, and you get a bonus on top of that for making it to the finale," she explained on The Morning After. "If you win, it's not like you win a $1 million and split it with your partner. You're just getting a cute trophy together.".

Do the Troupe Members Get Paid as Much as the Pros on Dancing With the Stars?

That doesn't appear to be the case.

On a 2022 episode of Trading Secrets, Lindsay Arnold recalled how her salary was cut "more than in half" when she was demoted from pro to troupe member.

How Are Pros and Celebrities Paired Together on Dancing With the Stars?

The pros get little input when it comes to being matched with a celebrity.

"You get no say," Lindsay noted on a May 2025 episode of Maggie Sellers' Hot Smart Rich podcast. "It's very much just, 'Here's your partner. Make it work.'".

In fact, Jenna said the pairing is often a secret until the last minute.

"They really want to keep it a secret until you meet them live," Jenna noted on The Morning After. "They want that genuine reaction. So I think people always think we know who we have and we're keeping it a secret. Absolutely not. They do not tell us. They really don't even want us to know the cast. It gets leaked a lot, but they want it very hush-hush until you walk in and meet your partner.".

As for what the Dancing With the Stars team looks for when making these matches?

Industry observers note that "It's based on height, build and personality and compatibility," former showrunner Rob Wade told E! News in 2015. "We don't pair people who aren't going to get on. It's too intense. It's not like The Bachelor or something, we couldn't do that. That would just be miserable experience for the celebrity, for us and the viewer. You don't want to see two people who don't like each other and, quite frankly, we have made that mistake pairing people up who didn't get on so well.".

How Often Do the Pros and Celebrities Practice on Dancing With the Stars?

Put simply, a lot."Every day we have four-hour rehearsals," Rylee Arnold, who was partnered with Olympic gymnast Stephen Nedoroscik on season 33, shared on a September 2024 episode of the Lightweights Podcast With Joe Vulpis. "It’s either 9:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m., 1:00 p.m. to 5:00 p.m. or 5:00 p.m to 9:00 p.m."But the work doesn't stop once the rehearsal wraps. Rylee noted she might then meet with producers or the creative team, work on choreography or study dance videos."Literally my whole life is devoted to it," she continued, "but it's my passion and it's what I love. So, it makes me so happy."Indeed, it's a no-days-off kind of gig."We have our show day on Tuesday and then it's Wednesday to Sunday, straight rehearsals," Rylee added. "And then Monday we have camera blocking and then Tuesday's show day again.".

Do the Pros Get to Pick the Songs Each Week for Their Dance With Their Celebrity Partner?

"Mostly yes," Emma Slater and Britt Stewart revealed in a September 2025 Instagram video, "though it's a collaboration with producers.".

What's the Process Like for Making the Costumes for Dancing With the Stars?

If you thought the quickstep was fast, just wait until you hear about the pace of the costume department."We meet with the set and lighting designers, dancers and talent and create a story [for each pair]," costume designer Daniela Gschwendtner told TV Insider back in 2017. "Then we sketch out ideas. We have five days, max, to make all the outfits. That’s half a day per costume, not including all the rhinestones. The fitting and trimming we do later. We have about 20 people in our department and then we have a separate tailor shop. It’s a massive enterprise."In fact, costume designer Steven Norman Lee mentioned pairs usually try on their costumes for the first time just hours before showtime. And while the department "might use a pair of pants again for the boys," he continued, everything is generally made custom each week.As Gschwendtner added, "We do reuse things for group numbers or promo shoots, but not for the competition. We don’t reuse things unless there’s a specific reason to do so. We try to keep everybody fresh and fresh in something different every week, so it stays interesting.".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, michael Giles, co-founder and original drummer of King Crimson, has died.
  • According to recent reports, giles died Monday (Nov.
  • “Michael’s originality, musical curiosity and uncompromising commitment to creative freedom challenged conventions and inspired generations of musicians around the world,” the label wrote.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, michael Giles, co-founder and original drummer of King Crimson, has died. He was 84.

According to recent reports, giles died Monday (Nov. 23), according to the band’s record label, DGM. No cause of death was revealed.

“Michael’s originality, musical curiosity and uncompromising commitment to creative freedom challenged conventions and inspired generations of musicians around the world,” the label wrote. “He leaves behind an extraordinary musical legacy, and his unique contribution to the evolution of progressive music will never be forgotten.”.

Industry observers note that born March 1, 1942, in Bournemouth, on England’s south coast, Giles began his music career alongside his brother Peter Giles and guitarist Robert Fripp. The three formed the rock band Giles, Giles and Fripp in 1967. The group released its only album, The Cheerful Insanity of Giles, Giles and Fripp, in 1968. The album helped lay the groundwork for what would become King Crimson.

According to recent reports, giles and Fripp went on to form King Crimson in late 1968, joined by bassist and vocalist Greg Lake, multi-instrumentalist Ian McDonald and lyricist Peter Sinfield. The band released its debut album, In the Court of the Crimson King, in October 1969, helping establish King Crimson as one of the pioneering acts in progressive rock.

King Crimson made its live debut in April 1969 and later opened for The Rolling Stones at their famous Hyde Park concert that July. Despite the band’s early success, Giles and McDonald left King Crimson during a U.S. tour in late 1969 to pursue a project of their own.

The pair released their debut album, McDonald and Giles, in 1970. That same year, Giles returned to King Crimson as a session musician for its second album, In the Wake of Poseidon. He also appeared on Epitaph, a live release featuring recordings from the band’s 1969 performances.

Giles went on to build an extensive career as a session musician, recording with artists including Steve Winwood, Bryan Ferry, Leo Sayer, Anthony Phillips, Kevin Ayers, Greg Lake, Neil Sedaka, Yvonne Elliman, Rupert Hine, Roger Glover, Francis Monkman, Andy Summers, Peter Sinfield and the Penguin Cafe Orchestra. He also collaborated with former King Crimson bandmates on their solo projects.

In 2002, Giles became a founding member of the 21st Century Schizoid Band, reuniting with former King Crimson bandmates to perform the group’s early material.

According to recent reports, giles continued exploring his own musical projects, including the Michael Giles MAD Band. His solo album, Progress, was recorded in 1978 and released in 2001. In 2026, he released Shadows/Solo, a collection of recordings spanning several decades.

Giles is survived by his five children, Tina, Amanda, William, Rosie and Oliver; his sister, Marion; and his brother, Peter.

How Jump-Roping Toy Soldiers Accidentally Took Over Your FYP

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1276 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Holidave, the stalwart leader of SeaWorld’s jump-roping toy soldiers troupe, is known for his ability to jump rope while sitting down, “a skill only shared by 0.1 percent of Earth’s population.”.
  • He’s the most “laid-back” of all the toy soldiers, allowing fellow toy soldier Jackary Jingleson to take center stage.
  • This is all according to AI slop videos posted by @wejumprope_memes, a fan page devoted to the group of masked professional jump ropers, who perform an annual holiday show at SeaWorld Orlando.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Holidave, the stalwart leader of SeaWorld’s jump-roping toy soldiers troupe, is known for his ability to jump rope while sitting down, “a skill only shared by 0.1 percent of Earth’s population.”.

He’s the most “laid-back” of all the toy soldiers, allowing fellow toy soldier Jackary Jingleson to take center stage. And “experts” and “recent polling data,” “fans believe it is Holidave who holds the most whimsy” out of all the SeaWorld toy soldiers.

This is all according to AI slop videos posted by @wejumprope_memes, a fan page devoted to the group of masked professional jump ropers, who perform an annual holiday show at SeaWorld Orlando. Per toy soldier lore, in addition to Jackary Jingleson there’s also Sugarsnookie, Soulja Toy, Substantial Chestnut, and Frosty McSleigh. And all of the edits are the same: an AI-generated narrator recites stats about the toy soldiers, such as their net worth and their vertical leap, as if they were elite athletes and not niche theme park performers.

Sources indicate that for the past two weeks, fan page videos featuring the jump-roping toy soldiers have been going viral, with @wejumprope_memes’ most popular video garnering 1.2 million views. In the comments sections, fans debate the merits and deficits of each toy soldier, declaring their allegiance to their favorite as if they were a ’90s boy band: “Jackery Jingleson is having a banner year! His speed is incomparable, his style undeniable, and his technique is utterly flawless,” reads one comment. Another disputes this, writing “Soulja Toy the underrated gem.”.

Mostly, people seem confused as to why these videos keep showing up in their algorithm and why they keep watching them. “I have a PhD and lecture at a university. And yet here I am,” one commenter writes on a video about whether Major Bounce, a fresh toy soldier, will show up for the 2026 season. (In a November 20 Reel announcing “major news for the jump-roping toy soldier community,” he finally did.).

As it turns out, there’s a simple explanation for the virality. @wejumprope_memes is run by Devin Meek, an Orlando-based professional entertainer who works for WeFlip, a production organization that produces acrobatics shows. But he’s now perhaps best known as his alter ego—Holidave.

Recent findings suggest that what started just a few weeks ago as him making memes to make his coworkers laugh has metamorphosed into an internet sensation, with the toy soldiers amassing a genuine, and ardent, fandom. “I really just made these videos for my friends in the jump-roping community,” Meek tells WIRED. “But I guess they resonated with more people than I thought.”.

Industry observers note that the videos are piggybacking on a larger—and increasingly absurd—trend of seasonal theme park employees going viral. In September, as WIRED previously reported, SeaWorld Orlando enjoyed a bump in ticket sales thanks to Just One More Chapter, a BookTok-themed Halloween scare zone at SeaWorld Orlando that featured swaggering bad boys from the romantasy genre flirting with guests. And last month, women on TikTok swooned over Archer and Fryboy, two performers at Hersheypark Halloween known for sliding around in kneepads wearing tactical streetwear and clown makeup, a practice known as “sliding.”.

According to recent reports, meek, who has been jumping rope for the past 20 years, was inspired to create the videos featuring Sugarsnookie, Jackary, and the like after seeing the success of Archer and Fryboy, who have a combined more than 3.1 million followers on TikTok. “It was such an interesting phenomenon, because I’m somebody who is in a very similar position where I work a few months out of the year as a holiday-themed performer,” he indicates. “So I got a kick out of it.”.

It has been revealed that meek already had an account, @wejumprope_memes, where he posted jump-roping fails and compilations. He posted one video on November 13 featuring old footage from SeaWorld Orlando, where he’s been performing with the other toy soldiers for the past six years. (The group got started during the height of the Covid pandemic—hence, why they wear masks during their demonstrates.) “Fryboy who? Move over, Archer,” it begins, before introducing the lore of Jackery Jingleson, the most “light-hearted, nonchalant” of the toy soldiers.

To Meek’s surprise, the video received almost a million views and 588 comments, most of which were not from fellow members of the jumping community but from total strangers. So Meek posted more toy soldier lore on his meme page, introducing Big Chestnut (“a powerful jumper”), Soulja Toy (the developer of the “Christmas Ice Storm 261”), Sugarsnookie (“the girl’s girl of the group,” who is dating Big Chestnut) and Frosty McSleigh (“he has the fastest salute time of all the toy soldiers.”).

Though the lore is fictional, it’s also based on the jumpers’ actual skills and personalities: the jumpers who play Substantial Chestnut and Sugarsnookie are actually in a long-term relationship, and Jackery Jingleson, perhaps the most popular of the group, once held the world record for the fastest jump roper in the United States. “Honestly, that makes [the popularity of the memes] even funnier to us,” he says.

Sources indicate that though some fans have speculated in the comments that the toy soldier memes are a marketing campaign for SeaWorld Orlando, Meek denies that’s the case: He doesn’t tag SeaWorld in the comments, nor has he been in contact with the theme park about his page. (SeaWorld Orlando did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.).

Recent findings suggest that “This is something that is so targeted to people who are internet-brained and have this ironic sense of humor,” he states. “And that’s exactly the type of person who’ll tune out immediately if they feel like they’re being sold something on the internet.”.

Recent findings suggest that others have even speculated that there is an actual feud brewing between the SeaWorld Orlando “jumpers” and the Southern California–based “sliders,” though Meek claims the rivalry is playful, and he has even reached out to collab with them. (The sliders may view it differently: So far, he says, they “don’t seem super interested” in joining forces.).

What has surprised Meek the most, however, is that very few commenters suspect that the toy soldiers themselves are behind the memes. In fact, he’s been shocked by how many organic meme fan pages have popped up within the past week, with people drawing their own fan art of Holidave saluting or Jackery Jingleson jumping. WeFlip has also been deluged with business inquiries: “People are like, how can we get Jackery Jingleson out here?”.

Essentially, what started as an inside joke within an extremely niche community has evolved into an inside joke for the internet at large. “I think people like the feeling of being in on a joke and being a part of it and building it up,” he indicates.

Recent findings suggest that so what’s next for the SeaWorld Orlando jump-roping toy soldiers? The rotating cast typically performs at the park on the weekends, ramping up appearances as it gets closer to the holiday season. #208157. Industry News: Who was buried in Westminster Abbey's Roman coffin? A 150-year mystery may be solved

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1085 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Who was buried in Westminster Abbey's Roman coffin? A 150-year mystery may be solved

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1085 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A mystery surrounding a skeleton discovered inside an ancient Roman coffin at Westminster Abbey may finally be approaching a solution, more than 150 years after the remains first attracted attention.
  • It has been revealed that the limestone sarcophagus, formally excavated in 1869, carries an inscription naming Valerius Amandinus, a wealthy Briton who lived in London sometime between 300 and 400 AD.
  • Sources indicate that now, fresh archaeological research points to a surprising explanation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A mystery surrounding a skeleton discovered inside an ancient Roman coffin at Westminster Abbey may finally be approaching a solution, more than 150 years after the remains first attracted attention.

It has been revealed that the limestone sarcophagus, formally excavated in 1869, carries an inscription naming Valerius Amandinus, a wealthy Briton who lived in London sometime between 300 and 400 AD. However, a large Latin cross carved into its lid dates to approximately the 10th or 11th century, suggesting that the person buried inside lived hundreds of years after the coffin was originally made.

Sources indicate that now, fresh archaeological research points to a surprising explanation. The remains likely belong to a prominent medieval monk, and researchers have narrowed the possible identities to two men who once led Westminster Abbey.

Two Medieval Abbots Emerge as Leading Candidates.

The newly introduced findings, published in the peer-reviewed Journal of the British Archaeological Association, come from Professor Warwick Rodwell, Consultant Archaeologist at Westminster Abbey.

Rodwell identifies Aelfwig, an abbot who died around 1020, as the strongest candidate. At the time, Westminster Abbey was a Benedictine monastery, and Aelfwig had served there as a monk before becoming its abbot.

Another possibility is Wulnoth, who succeeded Aelfwig and died in 1049. Both men are believed to have been buried at the Abbey, making either a plausible match for the skeleton.

"We have two viable contenders for the occupant of the sarcophagus," claims Professor Rodwell, Consultant Archaeologist at Westminster Abbey.

"We do not know the date of birth of either. But either would fit equally well if we assume the Abbot was in his early twenties when the appointment was made and close to fifty when he died.

"The fact Aelfwig was already a monk of Westminster might favor him.".

The elaborate burial provides another reason to suspect that the deceased held an vital position. Rodwell suggests that the individual was 'honored' with a 'fine sarcophagus', an unusual distinction that would be consistent with the status of an abbot.

Rather than commissioning an entirely upcoming stone coffin, those responsible for the burial apparently reused an existing Roman sarcophagus. The man's wooden coffin was placed inside it, and the stone lid was modified with a prominent Latin cross. This may represent an early example of recycling a valuable object for an entirely different purpose.

Newly introduced Excavations Reveal the Skeleton's Age.

Sources indicate that the Roman sarcophagus and its mysterious occupant have fascinated researchers for generations. Rodwell's latest conclusions draw on several investigations conducted with specialists over the years, including work associated with Channel 4's Time Team.

In 2009, the television program examined the archaeology and architecture of King Henry III's original sacristy, located along the north side of Westminster Abbey.

Sources indicate that the same area was the scene of an earlier accidental discovery in 1820, when workers encountered the Roman coffin and broke its lid into six pieces. The damage was repaired around the time the sarcophagus was formally 'discovered' in 1869.

More recently, Pre-Construct Archaeology, one of the UK's largest commercial archaeological and heritage organizations, carried out another excavation of the sacristy. Completed in 2025, the project was undertaken to support construction of the King Charles III Sacristy, a newly introduced facility at Westminster Abbey scheduled to open the following year.

As part of this investigation, human bone specialist James Young Langthorne of Pre-Construct Archaeology (PCA) conducted a fresh examination of the skeleton.

It has been revealed that his analysis indicated that the deceased was a man between 35 and 49 years old who stood approximately 5 feet 9 inches tall. These findings differ considerably from an assessment made in the 1800s, which described the remains as those of a 'robust young man' no older than 30 and approximately 5 feet 7 inches tall.

Carbon Dating Confirms a 1,000-Year-Old Burial.

One of the most vital clues came from scientific dating of the remains. A bone sample was submitted to the Scottish Universities Environmental Research Centre for radiocarbon analysis, which produced a date range of 987 to 1052 AD.

This places the burial firmly within the late Saxon period, centuries after the Roman sarcophagus was originally created. The dates also align with the deaths of both Aelfwig and Wulnoth, strengthening the case that the skeleton belonged to one of these medieval abbots.

"This confirms that the reuse of the sarcophagus, and the associated remodeling of its cover, occurred in the late Saxon period.".

The results provide scientific support for the theory that an ancient Roman burial container was repurposed to honor an key religious figure nearly 1,000 years ago.

A Skeleton Thought Lost Was Hiding in Plain Sight.

Sources indicate that the investigation also brought renewed attention to an unexpected discovery made in 2016. For years, researchers had believed that the skeleton was missing, leaving an notable part of the burial's history unresolved.

That assumption proved mistaken when the sarcophagus was transported to a conservation studio. PCA researchers removed its lid and were surprised to find an almost complete human skeleton still inside.

The examination produced another clue that Rodwell describes as a 'remarkable new discovery'. Inside the stone coffin, researchers identified the rectangular outline of a structure that had disappeared long ago. Its shape was preserved by a white residue left behind by lime, a material historically used in burials.

Rodwell believes the outline marks the position of the original wooden coffin that held the deceased before it was placed inside the Roman sarcophagus.

"Although no physical traces of that feature remained, it can only have been a timber coffin, which has completely decayed over the course of the seven centuries that the sarcophagus was buried in the sacristy courtyard," writes Professor Rodwell.

Sources indicate that together, the rediscovered skeleton, evidence of a wooden coffin, and fresh scientific dating have transformed researchers' understanding of this unusual burial. Although the man's identity has not been established beyond doubt, the findings suggest that a medieval abbot may have been laid to rest in a Roman coffin already centuries old.

Visitors can see the sarcophagus today in the Queen's Diamond Jubilee Galleries at Westminster Abbey.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When India's world chess champion, Dommaraju Gukesh, faced reporters at the pre-tournament press conference in Geneva on Sunday, there was no sign of the youthful, carefree energy one might expect from a 20-year-old.

"I don't think I'm here to defend anything—I'm here to win it all over again," he remarked.

Starting November 24, Gukesh will be facing challenger Jakhovir Sindarov of Uzbekistan for a purse of $2.5 million (€2.3m) in the World Chess Championship.

According to recent reports, gukesh captured the title in 2024, making him the youngest-ever world champion at just 18. Since then, however, things have not as gone well for the player known for his exceptional calculation skills and a penchant for risky moves. He currently languishes in 26th place in the FIDE world rankings.

Sindarov, who has climbed to number four in the world, told reporters that he only began training "seriously" last year and has learned a lot from observing the reigning world champion.

"He has a very good strength in typical positions, his calculation is very good, and Gukesh can fight until the end," Sindarov mentioned.

Former world champion Viswanathan Anand, who was also one of the world's best players as a teenager, is not completely surprised by Gukesh's lack of form over the past two years.

"He became the world champion (very young). So suddenly the responsibility is shifted onto you and even expectations," Anand told DW.

"Clearly he has deficiencies in his chess as is normal for someone who's 20, he's not had time to experience a lot.".

By the time he became India's first world champion, Anand was 37 – ancient by the age-standards of today's top players.

"With powerful chess software and global connectivity, it is easier for young players today to reach the top level," Jan Gustafsson, coach of Germany's national chess team, told DW.

"Online chess provides many more learning opportunities for talented players," added Gustafsson, who sees the recent movement at the top of the rankings as a "generational shift.".

While Norway's Magnus Carlsen, long considered the greatest player of all time, remains number one in the world rankings, he rarely plays classical chess anymore and gave up his world championship title after declining to defend it in 2023.

According to recent reports, now, young players—particularly from Asia—are pushing to the forefront. Alongside Gukesh and Sindarov, players such as Rameshbabu Praggnanandhaa from India and Nodirbek Abdusattorov of Uzbekistan—an emerging chess powerhouse—are considered contenders to win a world championship in the not-too-distant future.

"Broad social acceptance and state support ensure that children can focus on chess at a very early stage," Gustafsson said.

Sources indicate that another contender is Germany's Vincent Keymer, who at 22 is number nine in the world and well established among the world's elite. Most recently, Keymer and his teammates won a bronze medal at the World Team Championship, often referred to as the "Chess Olympiad.".

Additional reporting by: Thomas Lemmer.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, changes in cities’ ranks in the natural sciences are shown for 2016 to 2025, as measured by Share in the Nature Index. Beijing remained in first place, while five more Chinese cities entered the top ten during the period. Two US cities that were once in the top 10 have since fallen out of the top 20.

It has been revealed that the leading cities for biological sciences in 2025 are shown alongside their 2016 and 2025 adjusted Share in the subject. This is the most geographically diverse of the natural-sciences subjects, with four US, four Chinese and two European cities in the top 10.

In a recent development, chinese cities take all top 10 places in the chemistry rankings for 2025, shown here with their 2016 and 2025 adjusted Share in the subject. Beijing and Shanghai had the highest growth over the period among the top 50 cities in the subject, each increasing their chemistry adjusted Share by almost 900.

Beijing contributed 25% of China’s Earth and environmental sciences Share in 2025 — the highest percentage among the top-five cities in the natural-sciences and health-sciences subject areas. Among the top 10 cities in Earth and environmental sciences for 2025, Qingdao had the biggest percentage change in adjusted Share between 2016 and 2025, at 545.5%, and Beijing gained the most adjusted Share points, at 703.
